articles.title: Amazon tops Forbes’ list of America’s best companies, edging out Apple for No. 1
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Amazon is the best company in America, according to Forbes.
The Seattle tech giant took the No. 1 spot on the publication’s 2027 “America’s Best Companies” list, moving up from No. 2 last year and edging out Apple.
Three other Washington state companies landed in the top 50: Microsoft at No. 6, Costco at No. 13 and Alaska Air Group at No. 39.

Last year’s No. 1, Berkshire Hathaway, slipped to No. 4. Nvidia ranked No. 3 on the same day CEO Jensen Huang resigned, following his admission of an extramarital affair. JPMorganChase, Alphabet, Royal Caribbean Group, Walmart and Marriott International round out the top 10.

Now in its third year, the ranking scores thousands of the largest public and private U.S. companies on factors including customer and employee sentiment, financial performance, creditworthiness, cybersecurity and innovation. Forbes said it worked with 12 data organizations to build the index.

Forbes said Amazon’s financial strength and size, its standing in news and social media, and the range of voices across the company and its leadership lifted it to No. 1. Apple scored especially well on employee satisfaction, customer loyalty, financial strength and innovation.
Forbes also pointed to Amazon’s speed, citing a feature that lets customers shop by text message. An employee suggested it in October and it launched Nov. 6.

“Innovating for customers, doing it fast, working backwards from their needs, that’s really at our core,” Beth Galetti, Amazon’s senior vice president of people, experience and technology, told Forbes.
In its own blog post Thursday, Amazon highlighted everything from faster delivery and custom AI chips to warehouse robotics and higher pay for frontline workers.

The ranking comes after a year of workforce cuts at Amazon. The company eliminated about 30,000 corporate jobs in rounds announced in October 2025 and January 2026, including more than 4,500 in Washington state. Smaller cuts followed throughout the year, including layoffs of fewer than 1,000 corporate employees in October, mainly in its Stores unit.

articles.title: XML pioneer Jean Paoli’s startup Docugami acquired by Inveniam after open-source partnership
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Docugami , the Seattle-area startup led by XML co-creator Jean Paoli, has been acquired by Inveniam , a Detroit-area company that uses blockchain to help investors verify the data behind assets such as commercial real estate and private loans.
The deal follows a partnership this summer in which the companies released DGML , Docugami’s open-source format for turning business documents into data that AI agents can use and check.

Financial terms of the acquisition weren’t disclosed. All of Docugami’s employees are joining Inveniam, a Docugami spokesperson said. The team numbers about 50 including contractors. Paoli becomes Inveniam’s chief product and technology officer, and Docugami will keep operating from Kirkland, according to the announcement .
Paoli co-founded Docugami in 2018 after more than 20 years at Microsoft, where he helped create XML and the Office file formats.

The startup, based in Kirkland, Wash., raised a $10 million seed round in 2020 led by SignalFire, with backing from Bob Muglia, the former Microsoft executive and Snowflake CEO. Grammarly, the writing-assistant company now known as Superhuman, later disclosed that it had taken part in the round, its first investment in another company .
Prior to the acquisition, Docugami ranked No. 155 on the GeekWire 200 , our list of the Pacific Northwest’s top independent, privately held startups.

DGML labels each piece of a document by what it is — a base rent, a loan payment, a liability cap — so a single figure can be traced back to the page it came from. Inveniam records a digital fingerprint of each of those data points on its blockchain, called NVNM Chain, so any later change shows up.

Inveniam executives said Thursday morning on a livestream with Paoli that DGML solves a problem they’ve had in bringing on new clients: every client’s documents are different, which required templates and standard formats before the data could be used.
“One promise I want to make personally: DGML stays open and its openness is strategic to Inveniam,” Paoli wrote in a LinkedIn post .

Inveniam, led by CEO Patrick O’Meara, also acquired Mantra , a crypto company that provided the original technology for NVNM Chain, earlier this year. Mantra co-founder John Patrick Mullin said on the livestream that NVNM Chain will move to its own independent blockchain, with the main network expected to launch in the next few weeks.
Fees on that network will help fund buybacks of an NVNM cryptocurrency token, Mullin said. O’Meara proposed a separate session on when that token will launch.

articles.title: Nvidia’s interim CEO spent 13 years behind the scenes at Microsoft
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Colette Kress, named Nvidia’s interim CEO on Thursday after Jensen Huang’s abrupt resignation, spent 13 years at Microsoft earlier in her career, including four as chief financial officer of the Redmond company’s Server and Tools business.

But to say she was under the radar would be an understatement: a search of Seattle-area news archives turns up a single mention of her name from her Microsoft years, in a 2007 press release listing her as a presenter at a Hotel 1000 seminar on Microsoft’s budgeting software.

Of course, that’s to be expected. Divisional finance execs aren’t typically public faces at Microsoft or anywhere else. But now she finds herself in the global spotlight, running the chipmaker at the center of the AI boom — at least for the time being.

Nvidia announced Thursday that Huang resigned as president, CEO and a member of the board, effective immediately, following reports of an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials reportedly concluded was a Chinese spy, and a second affair with a direct report.

Kress will remain CFO while the board searches for a permanent CEO, considering internal and external candidates. Director Harvey Jones, the former Synopsys CEO, becomes Nvidia’s first board chair. Nvidia shares fell more than 13% in early trading.

Wall Street analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives & Co. wrote in a note Thursday morning that Kress has built “enormous credibility” inside and outside Nvidia. “We always believed she would eventually be CEO of a major public tech company, but she would have to leave Nvidia after many years there,” he wrote.

Kress joined Microsoft in 1997 after finance roles at Texas Instruments, and held senior positions in corporate planning and finance before becoming chief financial officer of the Server and Tools business, which sold Windows Server, SQL Server and Visual Studio. Her LinkedIn profile lists her as a Microsoft corporate vice president from April 2006 to November 2010.

Server and Tools was also a training ground for Microsoft’s current leadership. Satya Nadella took over the business in 2011, after Kress left, and used it as a springboard to the CEO job three years later. Amy Hood, now Microsoft’s CFO, served as its chief of staff earlier in her career.

From Microsoft, Kress went to Cisco as senior vice president and CFO of its Business Technology and Operations Finance organization. Nvidia hired her as CFO in September 2013, ending a search of more than two years.
Now as Nvidia’s interim CEO, her first major test comes quickly. Nvidia reports fiscal third-quarter results Tuesday, Nov. 17, with an earnings call scheduled for 2 p.m. Pacific.

articles.title: Nvidia founder’s wife faces spotlight that MacKenzie Scott and Melinda French Gates know well
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: As the fallout from Jensen Huang’s affair came to a head with his resignation as Nvidia CEO on Thursday, attention has turned in part to his wife, Lori Huang, who has stayed largely in the background during their 41-year marriage.

A New York Times profile , and other media coverage, placed Lori Huang alongside two familiar Seattle names — MacKenzie Scott, ex-wife of Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, and Melinda French Gates, ex-wife of Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates — as tech billionaires’ spouses who have faced infidelity playing out in public.

Huang acknowledged to employees on Sunday that he had been unfaithful to his wife. The admission followed Times reporting last month that a Chinese businesswoman he had become close to had been identified by U.S. officials as an intelligence asset. China has denied the espionage claims.
On Wednesday, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with an Nvidia executive who reports to him, citing five people who worked at the company.
Nvidia named CFO Colette Kress interim CEO. Kress spent 13 years at Microsoft earlier in her career.

Huang was worth about $145 billion as of Wednesday’s close, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index , nearly all of it from his roughly 3.4% stake in Nvidia. That figure doesn’t reflect Thursday’s drop: Nvidia shares fell more than 13% at the open, pushing the company’s market value below $4 trillion, CNBC reported . Huang’s fortune peaked at as much as $195 billion in May, according to Bloomberg.

More than half of his 922 million shares belong to a trust where he and Lori Huang are co-trustees, the Times reported, and she solely controls a separate trust holding about $5 billion in Nvidia stock.

Scott and French Gates each came out of their divorces with vast fortunes. Scott, whose split from Bezos was announced in 2019 , left with about $38 billion. French Gates, who divorced Gates in 2021 , received an estimated $25 billion in a settlement that was never publicly disclosed, The Independent reported .

Both have since steered billions into philanthropy. Scott has donated $26 billion through her organization, Yield Giving. French Gates left the Gates Foundation in 2024 with $12.5 billion for her own work.

George Rush, who co-wrote the Daily News gossip column Rush & Molloy, told the Times that the Huang situation differs from the Bezos and Gates splits in one key way: this relationship has the potential to move markets and carry global consequences.

There has been no report of any plans by the Huangs to separate. Lori Huang did not respond to the Times’ request for comment. In his message to employees, Huang asked for privacy for his family, saying they bear no responsibility for his choices.

The couple’s story has Pacific Northwest roots. Jensen Huang, born in Taiwan, was sent as a child to live with relatives in Tacoma, Wash., and later went to high school in Beaverton, Ore., according to Quartr . Lori Huang also graduated from an Oregon high school.

The two met in the early 1980s at Oregon State University, where Lori Huang, then Lori Mills, was one of only a handful of women studying engineering, the Times reported. They were paired as lab partners in an electrical engineering fundamentals class, and Huang later told OSU that meeting her was “the most important, single event of OSU, and of my life.”

After graduating and marrying, the Huangs moved to Silicon Valley to work as chip designers. Lori Huang worked at Silicon Graphics, where she earned more than her husband did at LSI Logic, he told The New Yorker in 2023 . Just before Nvidia’s founding in 1993, she gave up her career to raise their two children, Spencer and Madison, who both now work at Nvidia.

Huang has frequently credited her support. Speaking on a podcast in May , he recalled missing the kids’ karate tournaments while building the company and said she never complained. “That’s the gift that she gave me,” he said.

Lori Huang is president of the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation , which had $9 billion in assets as of 2024, according to the Times. The couple gave $50 million in 2022 to launch a research complex bearing their names at Oregon State. Last month, the foundation gave the University of Washington’s Institute for Protein Design, led by Nobel laureate David Baker, nearly 7 million GPU hours of cloud computing .

articles.title: ‘Water for life, not data’: Amazon data center plan draws Eastern Washington protests
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Amazon’s plans to build a data center campus near the Columbia River in Eastern Washington drew pushback Monday at a meeting of the Walla Walla County commissioners.

Some attendees held handmade and printed signs reading “Amazon lies,” “Big tech is shady. No more data centers” and “Water for life, not data,” according to the Walla Walla Union-Bulletin and its photos of the event.

The majority of the roughly 56 public comments were opposed to or had concerns about data center development, including worries about groundwater supplies, effects on agriculture and wildlife, and a lack of transparency, the Union-Bulletin reported. Supporters pointed to potential benefits from job creation and economic development.

The meeting highlighted continued resistance to data centers from communities concerned about higher electricity bills, depleted freshwater supplies and other environmental and social repercussions. Over the past year, tech giants including Amazon and Microsoft have pledged to limit those impacts and invest in host communities, but those commitments have not ended the opposition.

Elected officials are increasingly considering legislation and local ordinances to set standards and require greater transparency — an approach some tech leaders say could help address public concerns.

“There is a role for good laws, and if laws emerge that require that everybody do this work in a responsible way, I think that might be part of the solution,” Brad Smith, Microsoft vice chair and president, recently told reporters at a company event .

Commissioners in Western Washington’s Skagit County last month adopted significant restrictions on data center development. The facilities are prohibited in unincorporated areas, with some exceptions, and new caps on size and electricity usage will limit the technology to small-scale operations.

The planned Walla Walla County campus is one of two projects that would mark Amazon’s first large-scale data center developments in its home state. The second is in West Richland, part of the Tri-Cities. Amazon already operates smaller data centers in Washington.

The Walla Walla County campus would occupy roughly 134 acres at Wallula Gap Business Park, on property formerly owned by the Port of Walla Walla. Its three proposed single-story data center buildings would create about 120 to 150 full-time jobs, Amazon said.

According to a company fact sheet, the campus would use roughly 14 million gallons of water from the public utility to cool its equipment during its first year of operation. Amazon says it is working with the port to build a system that would replace the utility-supplied cooling water with nonpotable water drawn from the Columbia River. Wastewater from the campus “will meet industrial reuse standards,” the company said.
The campus would also use about 6 million gallons of utility-supplied water annually for employee needs.
Amazon’s fact sheet says the company will cover the electricity costs associated with the data center and that the “expenses aren’t added to the bills of local residents or businesses.”

The company is also working with partners to develop a nuclear power plant using small modular nuclear reactors near the Tri-Cities. The proposed plant could begin operating in the 2030s and “will provide net-new carbon-free energy for communities in the Pacific Northwest, including Eastern Washington,” Amazon said.

Despite Amazon’s assurances, many attendees at Monday’s meeting called for a one-year, countywide moratorium on new data center development, the Union-Bulletin reported. Commissioner Bertha Clayton said she would consider a pause on new applications to give officials time to draft an ordinance to better regulate the developments.

Clayton said zoning changes adopted now would be unlikely to affect the current phase of Amazon’s project. The other two commissioners have previously said they do not support a moratorium, according to the Union-Bulletin.

The proposal is undergoing an environmental review under Washington’s State Environmental Policy Act, or SEPA. The review will assess potential environmental impacts and identify measures to address them. It will also determine whether the project requires a more detailed environmental impact statement.

articles.title: Constellation Space launches its platform for managing fleets of satellites with AI tools
articles.author: Alan Boyle
paras: Seattle-based Constellation Space is rolling out its flagship software platform, which uses machine learning to streamline operations for fleets of satellites and the ground networks that serve them.

“We build models in-house for things like weather, attenuation, signal jamming, demand … and synthesize all of that to help operators understand what their ground contact plan looks like in the future, and how to optimize their fleets,” CEO Kamran Majid told GeekWire.

The Constellation Platform is tailor-made for a growing number of satellite constellations in low Earth orbit. Keeping track of thousands of satellites — and the best opportunities for downlinking data from each of those satellites — is becoming an increasingly complicated task.
Constellation Space, which was founded last year , draws upon Majid’s experience as a NASA engineering intern and as a software engineer working on SpaceX’s Starlink satellite network.

“At Starlink, I saw firsthand how manual mission-control processes break down as constellations scale,” he said. “I started Constellation to help smaller teams get ahead of link failures instead of spending their time rebuilding pass plans and recovering from outages.”

Majid’s fellow co-founders include chief technology officer Raaid Kabir , a veteran of Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin space venture, and Omeed Tehrani and Laith Altarabishi , who were previously software engineers at Capital One. “We’re a team of six people right now,” Majid said.

One year into its existence, Constellation Space has already gained traction. Several months ago, the startup said it raised $7.5 million in a seed round backed by Y Combinator, Nvidia, OpenAI, Samsung Next and other investors.

Majid said an early version of the Constellation Platform has attracted more than 10 customers, including Amazon Web Services. It’s also used by more than 20 academic institutions. “Our annual contract value this year is $2.25 million,” he said.

The platform combines forecasts for factors affecting satellite transmissions — including space situational awareness, weather conditions, signal-to-noise ratios, signal jamming and bandwidth demand — to predict how many gigabytes of data can be transmitted during a given pass. Operators can then use that data to optimize transmission settings and schedules.

Its machine-learning model is pre-trained on data from a global network of sensors. Once it’s deployed, the model adapts to each fleet’s specific hardware and ground stations. Constellation Space says satellite operators can boost downlinked data per pass by as much as 36%.
Majid said the journey from SpaceX to startup has been “really interesting.”

“The mindset is very similar,” he said. “I was previously an engineer. Now I’m finding myself in more of a business role. The mindset is just ‘first-principles thinking’ about everything. Eliminate all the requirements that don’t make sense before you even start to think about solving the problem. Those core tenets have stayed as we’ve progressed as a venture, and I think that’s been really important to our success so far.”
Setting up the startup in the Seattle area, where more than half of the world’s satellites are built , has also been interesting.

“We are a Y Combinator company , so we were in San Francisco for a couple of months, and there was a lot of pressure from the community in SF to have everyone be in San Francisco. We definitely felt that a little bit,” Majid said.

“But operating in the satellite sector of the space industry, Seattle is becoming more and more of a hub for the space industry in general,” he said. “Space companies are either completely moving here, opening up headquarters here, or just branching out here. It’s that, mixed in with Seattle just being known as a tech hub — and also, we all love Seattle.”

articles.title: Maintenance of automated trains
articles.author: Martin Pagel
paras: Sound Transit has recently reduced construction cost with smaller station designs (for example Alaska Junction) but their current four-car trains are 380ft long while Vancouver’s SkyTrains are only 280ft long. That still requires bigger, harder to locate, and more expensive stations. Due to automation SkyTrain can operate more frequently and therefore still handle higher ridership while providing higher convenience. Sound Transit has considered automation but is concerned about interoperability with current trains. They could add an operator on surface portions such as through Rainier Valley. If they would keep the Ballard line separate, then interoperability would not be an issue, but Sound Transit would need to worry about where to park them at night (“stabling”), clean them, and maintain them. When Sound Transit considered a starter line for Ballard, they concluded that they would need to build an operations and maintenance facility (OMF) in Interbay and that its cost would offset all savings. I gathered some ideas on how to potentially reduce such effort.

If you connect the Ballard (starter) line with the main line, you could still use the existing Central OMF in SODO. If such a connection is not feasible, then you could build a separate regular OMF or consider other options.

For maintenance, you could connect to the BNSF tracks at Interbay and SODO to move trains between the Ballard line and the SODO OMF during off-hours. As BNSF tracks are not electrified, you would need a separate locomotive to pull the trains. You could also truck the trains as these occasional maintenance events.
For nightly cleaning and monthly maintenance, you may still want a separate small cleaning center just like SeaTac airport cleans their people movers locally.

When Lynnwood Link opened, Sound Transit did not have enough stabling space at the Central OMF. They parked some trains at various stations at night . Operators had to pick them up there in the morning and park them there at night. Automated trains may operate through the night. If you do not want to operate through the night to maintain the tracks, you can park automated trains anywhere. They can wake themselves up in the morning, go through safety checks, and move to the first station by themselves. In fact, if Sound Transit wants to reduce service in the evening and start cleaning cars, they could send them to the OMF for daily cleaning and afterwards park them at any pocket track. If they want to reduce service further, they even reduce service to a single track towards the end of the line and use the other track for stabling.
This would reduce the size and cost of the OMF considerably. As automated trains can move (“shunting”) themselves in and out of the OMF, there is no need for shunting staff.
Sound Transit could even allow construction of transit-oriented housing above such facility as the Hong Kong MTA has done for example.
If Ballard trains don’t need to use the Central OMF in SODO, Sound Transit may be able to reduce the size of the Everett OMF. This may shift some of the cost.

I would hope by reducing the cost of the maintenance facility, Sound Transit would consider an automated Ballard starter line and shorter stations. Due to its lower cost, it could connect Ballard sooner and also be more attractive to riders due to its higher frequency and longer service hours.

articles.title: Wilson Makes First Veto As Mayor Count, Tweaking RV Parking Reform
articles.author: Amy Sundberg
paras: Four members of the Seattle City Council chose to uphold Mayor Katie Wilson’s first veto in her tenure as mayor, with Councilmember Rob Saka flipping his original council vote. Overturning the veto council would have required a two-thirds council majority – six votes.

Last week, Wilson held a press conference to announce she was vetoing Councilmember Dan Strauss’s bill that would have instituted a recreational vehicle (RV) permitting program with the goal of ultimately removing all RVs from Seattle’s streets. Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck and Saka flanked Wilson in a show of support.
Wilson signed the other bills in Strauss’s RV package.

“As the Mayor, it is my responsibility to ensure that our city policies and programs are feasible, are a cost-effective use of public resources, and have a reasonable likelihood of achieving their stated goals,” Wilson said at her press conference. “I vetoed this bill because I'm concerned that the permit program outlined in Council Bill 121283 does not meet that threshold, and I wanted to give the council an opportunity to consider an alternative pathway.”

Wilson laid out that alternative pathway for helping people living in their RVs at the press conference and signed an executive order to formalize her intentions. Wilson’s plan involves strengthening outreach and services for people living in RVs, including providing resources for service providers to help connect folks to RV safe lots, shelter options, and other services, to include the opening of Glassyards Commons, a combination of RV safe lot and tiny house village, later this month.

Wilson intends to include RV residents in the citywide by-name list that features in her new strategy for addressing homelessness, and she also expressed interest in learning how RVs are being used, including by those people who aren’t living in them or might be traveling for work, medical care, or in order to do caretaking.

The executive order also forms a working group that will bring together City departments and community partners to focus specifically on the neighborhood impacts and public safety issues that involve RVs in Seattle.

Earlier in the summer, Strauss had introduced a package of legislation he framed as designed to help people living in their RVs. The package included opening a new RV safe lot and providing RV storage for people who were interested in keeping their RVs while trying a housing option, in addition to the restrictive permitting program targeted by the veto, which opponents said would simply increase the number of unhoused people on Seattle’s streets.
Strauss’s permitting program wasn’t set to take effect until April 2027, which he said would give the City time to make any necessary changes.

“This time is incredibly important for understanding what rules have changed, for hearing, digesting, and learning about the concerns that we've heard from some today, to ensure that if we need to change this legislation before the April effective date that we're able to,” Strauss said before the original vote.

The Seattle City Council passed Strauss’s package of legislation on October 20, with the legislation creating the permitting program passing on a 6-3 vote. The three councilmembers from the progressive wing – Councilmembers Dionne Foster, Eddie Lin, and Alexis Mercedes Rinck — voted against the bill. Passing the bill with a 6-3 majority seemed to promise Strauss a veto-proof majority to ensure his proposal became law.
However, the six votes weren’t as firm as Strauss had thought.

Wilson laid out several concerns relating to the RV permitting program that she said ultimately caused her to change her mind on supporting it. The program as described in the legislation would have been complex, involving several departments as well as requiring the hiring of several new positions and containing ongoing enforcement responsibilities. Strauss insisted that the census of people living in RVs be only one time so as to not attract people from other places living in their RVs to Seattle, but such a census would be difficult to undertake while ignoring all future Seattle residents who might end up someday living in an RV.

The potential cost of the program was a concern in Seattle’s current tight budget environment. The City estimated that implementing the permitting program could cost more than $10 million, a number Strauss contested.

Other issues mentioned by Wilson included the legal risk to which the legislation might expose the City, the possibility the program would pull capacity away from other urgent public safety issues, and the risk that the program might actually increase unsheltered homelessness, as some advocates had been contending.
Rinck didn’t mince words in her speech supporting Wilson’s decision to veto.

“I am here today in full support of Mayor Wilson's action. She is vetoing a permit program that is harmful, costly, and impossible to implement, one that won't deliver on what it promises,” Rinck said. “She's issuing an executive order that will actually help move people out of RVs and into shelter and housing while addressing problematic and criminal activity. Seattle residents deserve a government that's honest about what a policy can do and can't do. When we pass a law, they expect it to work. They expect it to be enforceable, and they expect it to be worth what it costs them. A permit program that we can't staff, can't enforce, and can't pay for does not meet that standard.”
Wilson waited until the last possible day to use her veto power, with Saka changing his mind on his vote at the eleventh hour, demolishing the council’s veto-proof majority.

“I’ve heard from the Mayor about unreasonable expectations, the ability or or lack thereof of our City to actually implement something like this on such an ambitious timeline,” Saka said. “But more importantly, I heard a framework for an alternative proposal, an alternative solution that could potentially be stronger, more effective, [and] bring more people along. That's why I welcome the Mayor's initiative, and believe we should give this process a fair opportunity to succeed.”
Saka said he hadn’t viewed Wilson’s executive order until the night before she announced her veto.

Strauss complained that Wilson had agreed to sign his entire legislative package into law, and that it had been delayed this year because he had put her legislative priorities ahead of his own. Strauss also said that a work group was already a part of his legislation so changes could be made ahead of implementation.

“I feel like [Wilson’s] word has been disingenuous,” Strauss said at a press conference. “There have been a number of times that she's broken the promises that she's made to me or the commitments that she's made to me, and that's why I say I can't trust her word anymore. It's not just one interaction. It's been several, and it's been a pattern over time.”
Wilson told the press, however, that she had simply changed her mind upon receiving more information.

“I was not originally intending to veto this legislation, and before the passage of the legislation, my staff communicated to Councilmember Strauss that I did not have a plan to veto it, which was absolutely true at that time,” Wilson said. “Since then, as my thinking has shifted and I got into more of a posture of considering all options, we were also transparent in communicating that to his office.”

Alison Eisinger, the executive director of the Seattle/King County Coalition on Homelessness, said in a public comment this morning that over 4,700 letters had been sent urging the council to uphold the veto.

“This legislation, this specific piece of legislation of the six brought forward, is a ban,” Eisinger said. “The changes to parking rules and the permit program would have created a draconian ban on hundreds of people who live in the best shelter available to them. Voting to uphold the veto will demonstrate that together with all of us, you're committed to a Seattle where we work together to strengthen our community, resolve problems, and create a better housed future.”

When discussing the council vote on the veto, Strauss said he shared the concerns about the implementation of the RV permitting program, but that his legislation would allow them to get around a table and find solutions. Strauss didn’t explain why he didn’t address more of his own concerns before bringing his legislation forward for council passage.
Saka reiterated his desire to give Wilson’s plan a chance.

“In my view, we need more leaders at all levels of government to humble themselves if and when new information becomes available, and to make the best decision, do the greatest good for the greatest number,” Saka said.

“To say that a vote today to sustain the veto is a vote for a new path is duplicitous, in my opinion, because that report can be provided even before the check and adjust period is halfway over,” Strauss shot back.
Later in the meeting, Councilmember Eddie Lin pointed out this comment might be against council rules.

“I do believe we have a rule about not impugning motives of each other, and I just heard something about intent being duplicitous, and I just want to address that because I do think that it is impugning the motive of one of my colleagues,” Lin said.

“I, too, took some issue with some comments made towards the very end of this conversation, and you know, the Seattle passive aggressive, subtle slights, let's disagree on the merits,” Saka said. “Councilmember Strauss, you have a problem with me? I promise you, I'm not the one. You can take it up with me directly.”
Hollingsworth expressed her disappointment in the performance of the King County Regional Homelessness Authority and explained why she was still voting in support of Strauss’s bill.

“We cannot place all the challenges on Mayor Wilson and this administration. This has been going on for years, for years,” Hollingsworth said. “But I do believe that we have to move beyond intentions and focus on executions. So I do respect folks that come, I do respect that my colleagues have different perspective on this legislation, but I also believe that when we raise concerns about potential harms of a policy, we must equally be willing to confront the harm that is happening under the status quo. That is what's important.”

With the RV permitting program no longer set to move forward, Wilson will be convening her working group to look more closely at issues involving RVs. Strauss said he’ll expect a report from the group by January 15.

Meanwhile, Strauss still has to complete his duties as Budget Chair, with the council set to make their final budget vote on November 20. Strauss complained that upholding this veto will impact that budget plan, requiring changes to his balancing package presented last week.

articles.title: Katie Wilson Headlines Speaker Lineup for The Urbanist's Dec. 4 Holiday Party
articles.author: Diego Batres
paras: Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson and newly elected State Representative Jessica Forsythe are headlining the speaking program for our Winter Holiday Party on December 4 !
Mayor Wilson has been in office for nearly a year and will speak about this year's victories and what urbanists can look forward to in 2027.

Forsythe unseated Representative Amy Walen to earn the right to represent the 48th Legislative District (encompassing parts of Kirkland, Redmond, and Bellevue). She will discuss the progress being made on urbanist issues on the Eastside and what she hopes to tackle in Olympia.

For our pre-reception, which will run from 6pm to 7pm, we will hear from newly elected State Representative Kelabe Tewolde and newly elected Seattle City Councilmember Nilu Jenks, who will shed some light on what they have cooking in their first year in office. The Urbanist's publishing team will also share some remarks. VIP tickets also cover admission to the main event.

General admission begins at 7pm, with festive beverages and heavy appetizers provided. Swing by for an hour or stay for the evening; the main event speaking program begins at 7:30 pm, headlined by Wilson and Forsythe.
After the speaking program, there will be plenty of time afterward to mingle and enjoy the evening.
Venue space is limited. So, get your tickets while supplies last.

articles.title: Gyeok and its delicious Korean chicken noodle soup next for former Capitol Hill fine dining space
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: A Broadway restaurant space previously home to some of the finest neighborhood dining of the past decade is ready to hatch a new venture that represents a twist of two seemingly indomitable Capitol Hill dining trends.

The former home of five-star — and $$$$$ — Altura is being readied to become Gyeok , a new sibling restaurant to Broadway’s Busan Jeong , the Korean joint from global restaurateur Hoyeon Park that opened earlier this year on the east side of the street specializing in “Korean Pork Broth Rice” with savory soups, Korean dumplings, Korean pancakes, and specialties like blood sausage.

Another ripple in the wave of Korean-inspired openings is one thing but Park tells CHS Gyeok will also be part of another food and drink trend quickly changing the menus of Capitol Hill dining — chicken.
As with Busan Jeong’s focus around rich broth, Gyeok will specialize in Korean chicken kalguksu — “knife-cut noodle soup,” Park writes — and the Korean ginseng chicken soup samgye-tang.
There is a third trend in the mix, of course. The across the street opening will help the Gyeok and Busan teams with logistics and easy supply runs.

Altura and its sibling restaurant Carrello enjoyed a similar relationship until chef/owner Nathan Lockwood decided to move Altura across the street to take over the Carrello space this fall. After starting 15 years ago on the west side of Broadway, Altura now continues its award-winning tasting menu service while adding some Carrello touches in the much larger space on the east side.

We don’t know if Altura is serving any chicken these days but the rest of Capitol Hill sure is. CHS reported earlier this week on yet another new chicken joint opening up — Rizzo’s Crispy Chicken is taking shape next door to Dick’s Drive-in and part of a flock of new chicken-centered ventures now taking roost around Capitol Hill and the Central District.

Meanwhile, Korean food and drink has become a major component of the dining scene — with a little help from the yes-it-really-exists Korean Food Promotion Institute . As CHS wrote last year, knowing your way around a Korean spice rack is pretty useful on Capitol Hill. The Gol Mok Korean Market Bar holds down a space on E Pike . Yeobo Cafe and Bar and its Korean-American comfort food on E Madison is another addition. Another new joint , Seoul Mates , opened in a former sushi bar at 10th and Union. At the core, MEET BBQ from Heong Soon Park has grown into a center of the scene on E Pike.
The Chicken Food Promotion Institute could not be reached for comment.
Hoyeon Park tells CHS he is planning for Gyeok and its delicious Korean chicken noodle soup to debut in early December.
Gyeok will open soon at 617 Broadway E. Follow @gyeok.seattle for updates.

articles.title: Hope for art panels to be returned in Quality Flea Center heist
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: Thieves unbolted and stole eight original outdoor art panels from the Quality Flea Center events and community space on Capitol Hill overnight between November 6th and November 7th according to the venue.
“We’re heartbroken. And we’re pissed,” the shop wrote in a social media post following the theft. “Whoever took them came prepared.”

The 15th Ave E center that has made a multi-year run holding down the old QFC until a redevelopment of the block moves forward, commissioned local artist Ian Wheelock to create a 12-panel collection of hand-painted, sealed wooden character cutouts to brighten the sidewalk. Because the building’s textured anti-graffiti exterior prevents direct mural painting, the individual panels were bolted securely to the wall, requiring thieves to bring tools to remove them, according to co-owner Todd Hewitt.
Eight of the dozen one-of-a-kind pieces were taken.
Hewitt said the shop’s goal is to recover the work and return it to public view, offering no-questions-asked if the panels are brought back.
Anyone with information or who spots the artwork in the neighborhood is asked to contact the Punk Rock Flea Market and Quality Flea Center directly.

articles.title: Seattle to ease building rules for churches and daycares
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: As it pounds out its final changes to the city’s 2027-2028 budget, the Seattle City Council passed a bill this week opening up development standards for smaller institutional uses in multifamily zones throughout the city.

The bill from land use chair Eddie Lin is hoped to make it easier for neighborhood organizations such as churches, temples, mosques, childcare facilities, and community centers to find new locations, build, or expand by allowing the organizations to follow standard residential building rules rather than stricter separate regulations.

The bill will allow qualifying institutions to adopt the same setback, height, structure width, and structure depth limits that govern regular residential developments in the same zone. It will also remove buffers forcing institutions to stay at least 600 feet away from each other, while adding standard rules for greenery, landscaping, and screening around parking areas.

A late amendment restored landscaping requirements for surface parking lots, lowered the threshold from 20 to 12 parking spaces for those requirements, and increased the number of required trees for surface parking lots from one tree for every five spaces to one for every four spaces.

The passage comes as the council is focused on wrapping up the city’s long budget season with final adjustments to the mayor’s 2027-2028 budget plan including tapping $31 million in JumpStart payroll tax reserves and cutting $22 million in pension transfers to reverse cuts proposed by the mayor to address a looming budget deficit.

It also comes as the stalled council process to complete the city’s new comprehensive plan awaits a battle playing out in court over State Environmental Policy Act and Growth Management Act rules forced by anti-growth activists and conservation groups, including the Orca Conservancy, the Orca Network, and the Puget Sound Harvesters Association .

CHS reported here in December 2025 as the first phase of legislation setting the framework for the city’s new 20-year growth plan including state-mandated “Middle Housing” laws expanding zoning to allow a greater range of housing types in more parts of the city was finally wrapped up.

articles.title: AI Winter Is Coming
articles.author: Amanda Manitach
paras: Cam Smith helped create Siri. He worked in Silicon Valley for six years, much of the time at Apple, where he trained nascent language learning models to parrot human language and perfect the craft of next-word prediction. Like a lot of tech workers, he didn’t grasp the extent of the Pandora’s Box they were building at the time. He also couldn’t predict the way tech oligarchs would wield AI. When he finally quit tech two years ago to pursue making art full-time , he set out to use his toolset to expose the corruption at the heart of those corporations. “I view my art practice as critically engaging with technology—taking ideas and tools from the tech industry and exploring and exaggerating them to show their shortcomings and weaknesses,” he told me over email.

Tonight you can see Smith’s work at Passable Art in his solo show Surveillance State of Mind. The exhibit features many of the ideas he’s been pursuing in the past few years, including gutting and hacking Flock cameras to turn them into engines for new media art.

Unless you’ve been living under a rock, you’re probably aware that Flock cameras are public enemy number one (or a top contender at least) in Seattle right now. Seeing a real one up close and pulled apart in Smith’s Belltown studio is a little unnerving. For one thing, they’re big—large and Darth Vader-esque with their sleek black plastic casing and many-eyed, glowing red eyes that drill down on every ant-like human scurrying across the city’s crosswalks. Inside, there’s a computer, modem, and a brick of a lithium-ion battery pack. With Smith’s modifications, they become cameras for art. Hacking these machines is easier than you think, he would like you to know. (His are all ethically sourced, he assures.)

Smith’s work spans a range of interactive devices. One of his signature pieces is a Mona Lisa -inspired digital painting that uses generative AI in real time to melt Mona and meld the viewer’s face with the painting. It’s a very surreal and (at times) uncomfortable embodied experience—a digital reflecting pool that mirrors and morphs in response to your proximity to an invisible camera hidden behind the frame. But the image of you is never quite right or accurate, nor within the control of the viewer to manipulate. Smith poses the question: “If a random artist with a cheap computer can hijack the world’s most famous portrait in real time, what are tech corporations capable of doing with your data?”

Other works are more literal takes on the state of surveillance, compiling hours’ or days’ worth of surveillance data (read: individuals) crossing the street, collaged into beautiful kaleidoscopic compositions that pulsate and blink across a redacted, blacked-out background. In some ways, Smith’s work feels incredibly romantic, old-world, and painterly-coded; it also couldn’t be colder and more contemporary.

Smith’s got an analog side too. Earlier this year, he collaborated with AI scientist Myke Walton to write and publish the zine AI MUST DIE . Inside its radioactive Brat-green cover (featuring a photo of a security robot nose-down in a fountain), AI MUST DIE lays out the sci-fi fantasies and tech ideologies driving Silicon Valley’s relentless pursuit to take over every corner of our wallets and lives. It also contains a huge list of resources reflecting the growing AI resistance movement.

The zine keeps going viral every few months—this past weekend, thanks to a random post on X (a site Smith doesn’t even use). Smith estimates he’s sold or given away at least 4,000 physical zines to date, not counting the free version viewed online. (He can’t track that info because he and Walton “hacked the website together out of raw HTML in 15 minutes.” There are no analytics.)
Ahead of his show at Passable, Smith answered a few questions about his background in tech and the way AI resistance is shaping up in 2026.

How old were you when you first encountered AI and what was the context? I got really interested in cognitive science when I read How the Mind Works for a sixth-grade book report project. From there I got into Marvin Minsky and machine learning, but during this time period we were experiencing an “AI winter” and not much attention was paid to the field. After I dropped out of a PhD program, I found that some of the basic machine learning skills I’d picked up in cognitive science classes in college were in high demand, so I followed the money to Silicon Valley. I’m an atheist and materialist and was always interested in the “computational theory of mind,” but right now (2026) I’m worried that philosophical and technical discussions about AI systems are distracting from their real-world harms.

Were you ever excited about the potential of AI? Yes. Like many in Silicon Valley, I believed in the liberatory power of technology—techno-optimism. Techno-optimism has now evolved into its logical conclusion—effective accelerationism (or e/acc), which advocates rapid AI development regardless of the costs, with the belief that the benefits of AGI (artificial general intelligence) will outweigh any downsides. Some of these beliefs were easy for me to believe in the mid-2010s when I was working in tech—it’s easy to think the products and tools you’re developing are more important than the political and social work being done by others.

Is there anything you find good or useful about it? AI is a bundle of random tools. What they have in common is a metaphorical connection to “thought”—if you can describe your tool as “mind-like,” it’s AI. AlphaFold is an AI tool that mostly solved the protein folding problem, and its creator, Demis Hassabis, won a Nobel Prize for its creation. At the same time, the IDF uses an AI tool called “Gospel” for selecting targets as part of the ongoing ethnic cleansing in the Gaza Strip.

What spurred you to make the zine? 1) The rapid realignment of the tech industry and federal government under Trump. 2) My co-author, Myke, worked as a researcher at Census—policy work to help democratically govern AI. When Trump came back, Myke got the DOGE email from Elon and decided to quit. We had a few conversations. The word “zine” came up, and I convinced him to drive up from Olympia for a two-day intensive writing session at my art collective’s print shop (Common Area Maintenance).

The zine talks about hype cycles and AI winters. We’re currently in a hype cycle (the third one, according to you). Do you have a prediction for when the next impending AI winter will hit? As the saying goes, predictions are hard to make, especially about the future. What I’ll say is that an enormous amount of money and power is tied up with these AI tools, and it’s really important to talk about them in a way that’s critical and doesn’t hype up the product or downplay its real-world negative consequences.

When the hype bubble bursts this time around, will we be educated enough to get exactly what’s happening? Will we emerge from the next AI winter better equipped to resist the next hype cycle? I hope that more zines, podcasts, news articles, books, TV shows, etc., will be coming out that criticize and push back against AI, so that we can make educated decisions about how it’s used. The people boosting AI products are salespeople, not genius innovators, and we have to be careful not to get swindled—even the few genuine scientists in the space (Dario [Amodei], [Ilya] Sutskever, Hassabis) are too lost in the sauce. I spent years exploring and critiquing “alternative medicine” and “pseudoscience,” and when people are educated about these frauds, they start making better decisions that save them time, money, and prevent negative health outcomes—it’s the same story with AI products.

Do you think most people see through the hype at this point? Some do, some don’t. Most Americans have at least some intuitive sense that AI comes along with “bad vibes”—and some of us go further and explore why it feels so icky. But in my experience, a very sanitized and optimistic version of AI is exported overseas. I’ve had extensive conversations (workshops, talks, etc.) with organizations in Taiwan, and despite people there being highly educated, worldly, and technologically literate, few know anything about the ideological underpinnings of the Silicon Valley billionaires pushing AI. Even in Seattle, the AI ideologies exported here from Silicon Valley are highly sanitized—you have to visit a startup or a hacker house in the Bay Area to get the raw, unfiltered insanity.

Speaking of exposing the unfiltered, your zine traces the connection between Silicon Valley and eugenics—something that’s been substantially documented by folks like Valerie Veatch . Where do you see the eugenics thread showing up in our current moment, culturally? And what should people understand about it? You don’t have to look far to find evidence: Some of Seattle’s tech elite/art patronage has its own eugenics problem. If you can optimize and control some technology system, the thinking goes, why can’t you do it with the human race? Technologists are often smart and very good at solving technical problems, and have all the confidence that comes along with success in their field. But despite the STEM acronym, technology and science are very different—science, in the classic Karl Popper formulation, involves making theories that can be falsified by experiment in an attempt to better understand reality. In contrast, technology is about solving problems to get work done. Science involves lots of skepticism, critical thinking, and getting really deep into the foundations of truth and knowledge. Tech less so. So when techies wade into the intellectual waters of anthropology or biology, you get half-truths, misunderstandings, and nasty pseudoscientific frauds like eugenics.

Something else the zine calls out is liberal passivity: “Governments and corporations have demonstrated their total unwillingness, incompetence, and incapacity to meaningfully commit to accomplishing this goal.” Does that mean there isn’t much at this point we can do in terms of organizing political action? I think there’s a lot we can do. Continue holding governments and corporations accountable. Vote, and vote with your dollars too. The midterm “blue wave” was partly a repudiation of data centers—a very positive sign that when Americans are pushed to the brink, we can respond positively. But there’s also plenty of space for direct action—hacking and destroying surveillance systems, poisoning databases, leaking state or corporate secrets, if you’re involved in one of those organizations.

What about at the household level—is there a meaningful way to divest from AI? Harm reduction approach: Think of all the ways you use AI today and write down the alternatives. Start with the easy ones, like buying a cookbook instead of using ChatGPT to come up with meal ideas for you. Then move down the list until it gets harder. If you’re still using AI and have some technical background, think about running your own models instead of using Claude/Grok/whatever. Continually ask yourself: Am I using the tool in a way that gives me power and agency, or am I turning over power and agency to the tool? Do I need to use this? What are the risks and what are the benefits? Is this something that only belongs in the workplace, or should I use this at home too? Where is the data going? Who owns this tool? What do the owners and creators of this tool believe about the world, and are those beliefs aligned with my own?

Something pretty much everyone agrees on at this point (across the political spectrum) is that they don’t want data centers in their backyard. What does an effective revolt against data centers look like? This is something I’m optimistic about: Something like 40 out of the 41 anti-data center bills that were on the midterm ballot got approved by voters. It seems like there’s already momentum here, and I hope it grows into a bigger and more nuanced revolt against the tech oligarchy. On the other hand, we might end up in a Singapore/China situation: Jensen Huang, the CEO of NVIDIA, was recently caught having an affair with the leader of an offshore Singaporean data center company—this company buys GPUs from the US, sets up data centers, and sells compute to China, circumventing US sanctions on exporting chips to China. We might end up in a similar situation, with data centers setting up across the border in Mexico.

What are the top resources you recommend if someone wants to read up on AI resistance? The Nerd Reich by Gil Duran describes the rise of the tech oligarchy and its belief system. Empire of AI by Karen Hao focuses on OpenAI and Sam Altman; it also paints a picture of Silicon Valley belief systems. Valley of Death by Sharon Weinberger focuses on the convergence of private tech capital and the US military—an extremely important topic for the future of the anti-war movement.

articles.title: Slog AM: Mississippi Elects First Black Man to Senate Since Reconstruction, American Honors Veterans with Deportations, AI Mogul Resigns in Disgrace Despite Trump’s Support
articles.author: Cedar Attanasio
paras: Blue wave crests in Mississippi. The AP has called a 55th Senate seat for Democrats, NPR reports . Winner Scott Colom will be the first Black senator from Mississippi since Reconstruction and the white supremecist voter suppression that followed.

If you will it, it is no dream. In Georgia, columnist Charles Blow’s dream to reverse the Great Migration and reconcentrate Black voters in the South feels like it paid off. (Many have written about this but Atlanta Magazine has a more recent look summarizing Blow’s book The Devil You Know ). Black residents make a few more percentage points of the population in Atlanta now than in 2020 when he moved there. Of course, so did my Italian and Puerto Rican relatives from New York City, and they are also running up the score for Democrats. The state became a majority-minority state last year.

Alaska is still looking blue. Democrat Mary Peltola is beating both Dan Sullivans in the latest vote count, according to the Hill . She could be on track to win 50 percent of the vote, avoiding the complication of ranked choice voting. If she wins, Democrats will caucus with a 56-44 majority. Ballot counting is expected to continue into next week, as overseas ballots continue to add to the outstanding vote totals until Nov. 18 .

Seattle’s City Council is moving faster than normal to pass the city budget and could do so by Friday, PubliCola reports . The vote was originally planned for Monday—which is also earlier than the Council usually votes on the budget—but Budget Chair Dan Strauss moved it up.

BREAKING: Jensen Huang resigned today from Nvidia following an affair that threatened US national security. The suspected spy who shagged Huang was a Chinese tech CEO whose company was investigated for smuggling regulated Nvidia AI chips to China, and the New York Times has a liveblog on the aftermath . The NYT previously reported that Huang had been “affectionate” in a hotel with a younger VP who was his direct report . Huang called it quits Thursday despite a strong defense from Donald Trump, a fellow philanderer and Nvidia shareholder. The President feigning ignorance about the scandal is a reminder that he doesn’t care much about national security, The Atlantic Daily observes .

Why are we still calling this a ceasefire? Israel bombed another hospital in Gaza. Al Jazeera reports the air strike killed six Palestinians including a surgeon. Israel claimed it was targeting a Hamas commander holed up in the hospital. Even the Jerusalem Post acknowledged that Hamas hasn’t killed any Israelis in a while .

Veterans and their loved ones are still fighting against deportations. I covered so many veteran and spouse deportations carried out by Trump administrations that they don’t really count as news any more. But in honor of Veterans Day yesterday, here is the latest example from an 80-year-old Vietnam War veteran in San Diego whose wife was detained by ICE after living in the US for 25 years: “It doesn’t make a damn bit of sense,” Elton Stovell told CBS 8 San Diego . “I’m a senior citizen now. At least let my wife stay with me until I croak.”

They’re deporting the squirrels’… owners. A family that protested against New York officials when they killed their pet squirrel, Peanut, is angry at federal officials after one of them landed in immigration jail, the AP reports . The German woman who co-owned Peanut with her American husband is not the wurst of the wurst. And the couple’s activism and social media activity around the squirrel had become a political rallying cry for JD Vance during the campaign: “ The same government that doesn’t care about hundreds of thousands of illegal immigrant criminals coming into our country doesn’t want us to have pets. It’s the craziest, the craziest thing ,” Vance said in 2024 .
(This blurb has been updated to correct the gender of the person detained)

A Bellevue man is suing Kalshi under a Washington law that bans online gambling . He’s asking a judge to hit Kalshi for his sports betting losses totalling over $300,000, Ars Technica reports . Addiction is a bitch, right? So is civil litigation. That opens a new can of worms for gambling site Kalshi, which claims prediction market betting isn’t gambling. Washington State officials are already suing the company for violating its state online gambling laws. I’m hoping the court will at least return the $90,000 in fees they made off the guy over his many sports bets.

Will Seattle host the Women’s World Cup? We’re in the mix for hosting some games in the 2031 tournament, t he Seattle Times reports . Atlanta is already promised to host the final, but semifinal games might come to Lumen field, the paper says.

Outbreak alert: A dairy worker died after contracting bird flu amid a Yakima Valley outbreak, according to a United Farm Workers BlueSky post. The union says that “It is clear that most workers are not being informed of the risks of handling sick cattle and infected milk. They are being given no information on flu shots or avian flu testing.”

You can recycle electronics in SoDo on Saturday, Nov. 14. Friendly Earth Int’l is taking items at their Seattle Warehouse at 1560 1st Ave S from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m., I learned from a post in West Seattle Blog . Friendly Earth claims to dispose of e-waste without letting it end up in a foreign landfill and doesn’t use child or prison labor. It’s the little things.

Washington, you are relatively so hot right now. Major cities around the Puget Sound broke heat records relative to this time of year on Wednesday, KING 5 reports . It was 66 degrees at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport, breaking the 1990 record high of 65 degrees. It’s a reminder that this winter’s weather is gonna be whacky.

articles.title: Free Will Astrology
articles.author: Rob Brezsny
paras: ARIES (March 21-April 19): There is an old way of making fire: Strike a sharp edge of flint in a hard, glancing blow against steel. The flint shears off small particles of metal. Heated by the blow and exposed to air, they oxidize so swiftly that they burn as sparks. The fire is born from the fierce meeting of two hard things. This is a fitting emblem for you, Aries. Your fire often comes alive through bold contact, like a decisive strike or a willingness to meet resistance head-on rather than avoiding it. In the coming weeks, seek out, enjoy, and use the friction that ignites you. Find worthy flints and make sparks. Some fires can only be lit by impact.

TAURUS (April 20-May 20): A ship’s anchor doesn’t work by weight alone. Some of its holding power comes from how its blades dig into the seabed. A heavy anchor sitting on smooth rock is useless; a lighter anchor that catches in mud or sand can hold a massive vessel against storms. So the anchor’s value resides as much in its grip as its mass. Regard this as a useful metaphor, Taurus. Don’t try to hold yourself in place through sheer gravity, with accumulated possessions and commitments piling up like ballast. You need to hook yourself into a strong foundation.

GEMINI (May 21-June 20): Editors of dictionaries continually add new words while retiring obsolete definitions. Language remains vital and wild because it adapts to shifting realities. In that spirit, I invite you to eagerly edit the words you speak and the concepts you use to interpret your experience. Maybe you’ve attached labels to yourself that have become outdated. For example, you’re “multifaceted,” not “scattered.” One of your relationships isn’t so much “complicated” as “intricate” and “evolving.” A feeling you call “confusion” might be more accurately named “curiosity.” Fresh vocabulary may unlock intriguing and catalytic possibilities.

CANCER (June 21-July 22): When a Pakistani student named Malala Yousafzai was 11, she became a passionate advocate for female education. Girls had been banned by the Taliban from attending school in her native district. Her tireless work in this righteous cause angered conservatives, and at 15, she was shot in the head by a would-be assassin. Yet she survived and prevailed, redoubled her efforts, and at age 17, she became the youngest person to win a Nobel Peace Prize. Since then, she has continued her quest to aid girls and women, and extended her activism to assist refugees and immigrants. Can you guess her astrological sign? Cancer, of course. Who nurtures and protects so fiercely? Who fights tenderly for people in need to be safe and free? Now is an excellent time to decide how you can be inspired by Malala.

LEO (July 23-Aug. 22): During my first show as a lead singer for a rock band, age 19, I was absurdly anxious about hitting every note perfectly. Afterward, a friend critiqued my performance, saying I seemed locked up inside my own head. The next time I took the stage, I sang looser, sloppier, and wilder. I focused on connecting with the audience and allowing their enthusiasm to feed my energy. Much better! My technical execution was less than perfect, but I was far more engaging and entertaining. I dare you to apply this lesson to your own life in the coming weeks.

VIRGO (Aug. 23-Sept. 22): I advocate giving people the resources they need when they’re experiencing scarcity or deficiency. I also believe that exceptional ability deserves encouragement and support to thrive and ripen. That balance offers a useful way to think about your life right now. You’ve devoted plenty of attention to the parts of yourself that need help, while giving too little care to the parts that shine. To restore the balance, I suggest you seek out tools, teachers, and adventures that will challenge and nurture your talents. A gift that comes naturally isn’t a finished achievement. With practice, it can become even more extraordinary.

LIBRA (Sept. 23-Oct. 22): Libran poet Ocean Vuong describes tenderness as a courageous force rather than a sentimental one. Please try out this idea. Imagine the ways that gentle devotion and creative affection mobilize your most interesting strengths. Explore how your ability to express nourishing kindness empowers you to spawn wonders and marvels. Remember that water, yielding and supple, can reshape mountains and carve canyons. Your tenderness, too, may have the patient power to transform what seems fixed and unyielding.

SCORPIO (Oct. 23-Nov. 21): Some of our most powerful medicines come from feared venoms. A compound from the deadly cone snail became a painkiller stronger than morphine. Venoms from vipers and lizards have yielded drugs that treat blood clots and diabetes. The very chemistry that evolved to harm, once understood and transformed, becomes the chemistry that heals. This is your native alchemy, Scorpio. You grasp, as few others do, that the dangerous and the toxic can be transmuted into potent medicine when wrangled with courage and skill. But wait! Stop! None of this will be relevant for you in the coming weeks. Some of your best medicines will be sweet, agreeable, pleasant, and filled with light. I invite you to expand beyond your usual attitude and approach.

SAGITTARIUS (Nov. 22-Dec. 21): Sagittarian novelist Jane Austen wielded her drollery with aplomb. In a letter to her sister, she wrote, “I do not want people to be very agreeable, as it saves me the trouble of liking them a great deal.” Over two centuries later, I still find that joke funny. Jane was a wickedly independent spirit who refused to sugarcoat the raw truth or perform affection she didn’t feel. Let’s make her your guardian spirit for the coming weeks, Sagittarius. I hope she’ll inspire you to leaven your honesty with humor and liberate yourself from the need for people’s approval. Can you be blunt and genuine with wit and grace? I think you can. Feel no obligation to like or praise what hasn’t earned it.

CAPRICORN (Dec. 22-Jan. 19): Who are your favorite wild women? One of mine is Capricorn magician Patti Smith, whose untamed creativity has inspired me for years. At the root of her output as a musician and writer is her disciplined devotion: decades of patient, faithful labor at her craft, never chasing trends, simply doing the deep work year after year. She has been experimental and diligent; iconoclastic and tireless; one-of-a-kind and collaborative. I salute her contributions to my life and encourage you to be inspired by her skillful weaving of hard work and soulful expression.

AQUARIUS (Jan. 20-Feb. 18): Aquarius-born inventor Thomas Edison treated failure as useful information. He tinkered with thousands of materials as he sought a workable lightbulb filament. After each dud, he insisted he hadn’t misfired but had just found another way that didn’t work. Eventually, his numerous failures cleared his path to creating the lightbulb. In the coming weeks, I propose that you make him your role model, Aquarius. Your inventive, future-facing mind will be at its best when it treats setbacks not as verdicts but as data, clues pointing toward the solution. The breakthrough you’re in quest of will come just past the last dead end.

PISCES (Feb. 19-March 20): The painter Henri Matisse said he wanted his art to provide “a soothing, calming influence on the mind.” Yet his work shimmered with bold color and daring composition. Joyful vitality spilled out of his creations. For him, serenity wasn’t bland. I’d love for you to incorporate his attitude and approach in the coming weeks. There will be no need to choose between excitement and peace. You can attract experiences that are simultaneously stimulating and harmonious. My advice: Expect and pursue intriguing adventures that leave your nervous system feeling nourished.
Homework: What’s the smartest gamble you could take?
