articles.title: As Funds Dried Up, Nonprofit Immigration Group Hired Anti-Labor Law Firm to Crush Union
articles.author: Cedar Attanasio
paras: As the two executives of immigration advocacy group Washington Immigration Solidarity Network (WAISN) burned through cash and as donations dropped, a unionization effort from their workers led them to do something unthinkable for a Washington nonprofit allied with labor unions. WAISN hired Davis Grimm Payne & Marra, a top union-busting law firm in the Pacific Northwest whose work has eroded unions’ right to strike across the US.

The “Network” in WAISN’s name includes labor unions, including MLK Labor, a Seattle-based AFL-CIO affiliate that’s on WAISN’s steering committee, which advises the nonprofit. MLK Labor only learned about WAISN retaining the law firm from The Stranger ’s inquiry.

“MLK Labor supports every worker’s right to organize and form a union at every employer, no exceptions. Workplace democracy is a foundational workers’ right,” said Katie Garrow, MLK Labor Executive Secretary-Treasurer. “Your email was the first I heard that WAISN hired Davis Grimm. If that’s true, that’s extremely disappointing.”

Another steering committee member who advises WAISN, the Church Council of Greater Seattle, called the hiring of this firm “disturbing” and they feel workers’ “dignity and labor have not been honored.”

During the course of reporting this story, The Stranger reached out to some members of the WAISN board, and learned that two of the five board members resigned “recently.” One board member declined to comment for this story when reached by phone, and announced his resignation the next day, citing continuing health issues. It’s unclear if the other board member resigned before or after the revelation.

The contract between WAISN and the firm was discovered in open government records by the nonprofit watchdog LaborLab, and confirmed by The Stranger . Using publicly available rates information, LaborLab estimated WAISN paid around $20,000 to the firm to carry out the layoffs at the end of September, which The Stranger reported .

“Rather than investing that energy in collaboration, transparency, and protecting the services communities depend on, leadership chose to direct resources toward… preventing workers to fully exercise their collective rights,” the WAISN Worker Collective representing the nonprofit’s aspiring union members said in a statement.

WAISN’s directors hired the law firm—which they said in an email statement was one of six they interviewed—after a year of hemorrhaging cash. Failing to meet fundraising targets and unwilling to curb spendy events, the organization had already lost 71 percent of its cash on hand, according to a previously unreported budget document obtained by The Stranger .

This story also relies on accounts of five people affiliated with WAISN who are referenced anonymously due to fear or retribution by WAISN’s co-directors, who routinely required non-disclosure agreements as a condition of employment, and non-disparagement agreements as a condition of layoff benefits.

According to two people working at WAISN at the time the firm was hired, executives at the nonprofit blamed workers directly for having to spend the money on the firm, saying it was their fault for trying to unionize. They told workers it was to ensure that nobody’s rights were violated.

Davis Grimm Payne & Marra is particularly known in the labor movement for its representation of Glacier Northwest, a Washington subsidiary of West Coast cement giant CalPortland in their lawsuit for damages against the Teamsters filed after striking workers walked off the job with wet cement still in their trucks. While the Washington State Supreme Court followed precedent keeping most labor arbitrage under the purview of the National Labor Relations Board rather than the legal system, the United States Supreme Court disagreed.
The nation’s top justices ruled in favor of the cement company in 2023, a major blow to organized labor, which lone dissenting Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson said would “erode the right to strike.”
“Retaining the firm does not mean WAISN endorses the positions taken by its other clients,” WAISN said in the email, adding the firm was willing to start “within the timeframe we needed.”

According to US Department of Labor (DOL) records, the law firm has helped dozens of corporations oppose employee union campaigns and pressure workers to take management’s side during collective bargaining over the past decade and a half. The firm’s clients include the Washington Center for the Performing Arts, Sound Publishing (the largest owner of small newspapers in the state), Paratransit Services, Big Brothers and Big Sisters of Puget Sound, and many others.

On their website , Davis Grimm Payne & Marra offers to train employers in topics such as “How to Legally Respond to a Union Organizing Drive,” Understanding Why Employees Unionize,” and “Negotiating a Pro-Management Collective Bargaining Agreement.”

For instance, US DOL records show Davis Grimm Payne & Marra worked recently with Spokane green energy contractor Northwest Renewables to “persuade employees to vote ‘no’ and explain disadvantages of union representation” during a union drive by the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers Local 713. Despite nearly $8,000 worth of lawyering, the workers voted to unionize.

As for what services Davis Grimm Payne & Marra provided to WAISN, DOL records list the immigrants rights nonprofit paying the union-busting firm “$150 per hour to $425 per hour” after the WAISN Workers Collective organized to “persuade employees to exercise or not to exercise, or persuade employees as to the manner of exercising, the right to organize and bargain collectively through representatives of their own choosing,” and “explain advantages and disadvantages of union representation.”

“During this challenging time for the organization, we hope the focus can stay on the immigrant and refugees that WAISN serves. Immigration enforcement activity is increasing in Washington,” WAISN Board Chair Faiza Duale said in a statement. “We appreciate the cooperation, support, and solidarity of the community at this time.”
Duale says the board is committed to keeping WAISN’s programs and resources running.

WAISN’s Deportation Defense Hotline that used to answer calls from concerned migrants is still operating. But due to laying off all operators it’s only taking calls from 7 a.m. through 2 p.m. That’s hobbled its ability to answer calls and make resource referrals, for which the City of Seattle is paying the organization $22,000 this year, according to details of a $50,000 contract provided by the Office of Immigrant and Refugee Affairs (OIRA).

The hotline was also an organizing tool for mobilizing to quickly help communities following ICE activity. For example, volunteers observed police activity, helped secure vehicles, or put loved ones in touch with a detainee. WAISN used to coordinate these actions on a daily basis, but virtually never do anymore, says laid-off Rapid Response organizer Alex Fayer, one of at least three laid-off workers who have gone public after refusing to sign a non-disparagement during the layoffs.

“WAISN inadvertently left me in an internal Signal chat,” Fayer says. Despite being laid off in September, Fayer had access to a Signal chat until last week, which gave him “direct visibility into the dramatic collapse of WAISN’s rapid response capacity from the layoffs.”

The Stranger confirmed the shift with members of ICE observer groups across King County, which have pivoted to reporting ICE activity internally instead of calling the hotline, but have some communication with remaining WAISN staff.

WAISN is still carrying out programs funded by Seattle’s OIRA and pro-immigrant nonprofits. They successfully administer bonds to immigrants seeking release from detention, according to groups who have made referrals. WAISN still hosts online legal resources and pair accompaniment volunteers to go with immigrants to ICE check-ins or visit them in immigration detention.

The budget obtained by The Strange r documents plummeting cashflows. The organization blamed the layoffs on a drop in institutional funding, which had spiked after Trump unleashed his mass deportation agenda in 2025. WAISN leadership haven’t held a town-hall-style forum to discuss their finances, and it’s unclear how many months of runway they have after laying off 18 people—nearly half of their staff—this year. Most of those laid-off staff made between $70,000 and $75,000 annually.

The board says the directors had their pay cut, though declined to provide proof when The Stranger asked for pay stubs. The co-directors were each making $185,000 at the start of the year, according to two people familiar with the salaries. If they took the pay cut, reportedly 25 percent, in September, their salaries are now a combined $277,500 per year.

Internal financial records obtained by The Stranger suggest they may have painted themselves into a corner financially. They started 2026 with more than $3.5 million cash and were down to around $1 million in September, only 29 percent of their starting funds, according to an approved FY2026 budget authenticated by a third party. A DC-based spokesperson for WAISN did not dispute the authenticity of the document.
WAISN’s board says they approved the budget knowing they would spend more than they would raise, and points out that many other nonprofits do this.
But two former workers with knowledge of the company’s operations say that the directors ignored direct warnings in the spring that the organization was in poor financial health.

Members of the WAISN Worker’s Collective say the directors wasted a lot of money this year, even after they knew what they were facing. They point to event spending in August that would lose the organization $60,000, according to the budget document, and a failed fundraising strategy that shelled out a $360,000 annualized salary to a grant-writing consultant who didn’t appear to achieve much. And earlier in the year they spent $35,000 on recruiting director-level positions that were likely laid off or never filled in the first place.
Laid-off workers say more of the financial issues, and the cuts to services, should be released and discussed with stakeholders.

“The distrust WAISN is experiencing within its community and among its partners is not something that appeared overnight. It is the result of leadership decisions and a continued unwillingness to meaningfully engage with the people who have built, maintained, and relied on these programs,” the WAISN Worker’s Collective says.
Correction: This article has been corrected to reflect attribution of the WAISN leadership statements, which all come from the board, not the co-directors.

articles.title: Steph Curry’s defense of Ayesha exposes the ugly double standards of sports’ manosphere | Andrew Lawrence
articles.author: Andrew Lawrence
paras: The Warriors superstar’s forceful defense of his wife over an on-screen kiss has exposed the ugly double standards and fragile masculinity of sports’ manosphere

If Steph Curry is leading with his full government name, know that he means business. In a 90-second video released on Wednesday , from the Instagram account of “Wardell Curry”, he put the internet trolls who have been attacking his wife for years on notice. “Usually the noise doesn’t bother me, doesn’t bother Ayesha,” the four-time NBA champion and Paris Olympic knockout artist said. “But when you’re trying to step on the accomplishments of my wife, and feel the need to have to jump in and give an opinion on something that you really don’t know about, [it] kind of speaks to the bigger conversation on how you view women in this world and what they’re allowed and what they’re not allowed to do.”

Posterity will remember this as the NBA’s Oscar slap moment, but without the unnecessary violence. A bizarre turn in the parasocial compact when the restless fanboys pressured a superstar into publicly defending his wife. On this occasion, Curry had to defend his wife for the heinous crime of being the leading lady in a Christmas romcom: a Hallmark knockoff called Second Chance Holiday in which Ayesha Curry plays a dating expert with bad holiday luck and shares a kiss with a man who is not Wardell Stephen Curry II – her husband of 15 years and father to their four children. That apparently was a bridge too far for some of Curry’s former NBA peers.

articles.title: ‘To them, we’re just NPCs’: the artists and activists challenging Trump’s video game propaganda
articles.author: Alyssa Mercante
paras: Order a Diet Coke or invade Iran – that’s the choice facing the US president in one of several satirical games, as designers turn the gamification of politics back on the White House

In early September, the Trump White House announced a surprising new addition to its official website. Named simply Arcade , it is a collection of browser games based on classic titles such as Flappy Bird, Snake, and Tetris, but re-tuned as flagrant works of political propaganda. Designed to court reactionary gamers, they push the administration’s policies on immigration and other hot-button issues, while dehumanising their targets. There have recently been some new additions: a Temple Run clone named Red Scare about crossing the “ration market” and escaping the Democratic Socialists of America, and another simple item-matching game about the threat of socialism. In the midst of increasing fuel, utility and grocery prices thanks to the Iran war, these were naked attempts to distract voters by appealing to their video game nostalgia.

After an explosion of news coverage, Arcade caught the attention of the games industry. The Tetris Company warned on social media that it “took copyright infringement very seriously.” Days later, the game was removed from the White House site. However, aside from a March 2026 statement from the Pokémon Company condemning the White House for using its characters in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) propaganda, major video game companies have been relatively silent in the face of the administration’s widespread usage of their IP.

articles.title: ‘Maga is dead, Maga is effeminate’: why has the manosphere rejected Trump?

paras: As public mood has shifted on Israel-Gaza and the Iran war, so has the manosphere’s devotion to the US president

Earlier this week, Donald Trump announced that the UFC president, Dana White, was to become his press secretary. The US president hoped the creator of Power Slap, a face-slapping league which one of the world’s leading neurologists called “a sport inconsistent with the intelligence of humans”, might be the right man to deliver his daily rebuttals to the media.

Trump later backtracked on the appointment, saying he was “only kidding” , yet it is easy to understand why he might be pining for White’s muscles, trash talk and thirst for athletic violence. White is representative of the way Trump transcended politics in 2024 to become a celebrated figure in the manosphere, the loosely defined cluster of male content creators who have a direct line to America’s bored and aggrieved young men. On the night of the 2024 election, White stood at the victory podium reading out “thank yous” to the formerly heterodox podcast bros who came out for Trump: “the Nelk Boys, Adin Ross, Theo Von, Bussin’ With The Boys, and last but not least, the mighty and powerful Joe Rogan”. Trump ended up winning 63% of young white men that night, unheard of for a Republican politician.

articles.title: From ancient Asia to the AI age: Has China’s ‘beauty stratagem’ found a new victim in Nvidia’s Jensen Huang?
articles.author:
<name>Linggong Kong, Ph.D. Candidate in Political Science, Auburn University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/linggong-kong-2265722"/>
paras: Extramarital activities have led to the resignation of one of America’s most influential tech bosses, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The saga has also raised the specter of an age-old spying tactic: the “honey trap.”

Huang stepped down following media reports of an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, a Singapore-based executive suspected of having ties to Chinese intelligence agencies . She previously worked for Megaspeed, a cloud computing company under U.S. scrutiny for allegedly helping China obtain restricted AI chips.
Jensen Huang acknowledged an affair . And amid reports of a second with a company executive who reports to him , he tendered his resignation to the Nvidia board on Nov. 12, 2026.

The sensitivity of Huang’s work – AI is increasingly seen as central to national security – has turned a company matter into an international issue. China’s Foreign Ministry has denied the espionage allegations and accused the U.S. of “fabricating so-called spy narratives and ⁠⁠⁠⁠using them as a pretext for imposing ⁠⁠⁠⁠a technological blockade.” Nvidia says it has no reason to believe company secrets have been leaked.
Yet part of what makes the accusations so believable is history is dotted with examples of men being distracted, compromised or spied on by attractive men and women deployed for that purpose.
Indeed, in China it recalls an ancient political tactic known as “meiren ji” or the “ beauty stratagem .”

As a scholar specializing in U.S.-China relations , I believe that regardless of the particulars of the Huang case, the political logic behind the beauty stratagem – using personal relationships to obtain information, influence decisions and weaken opponents – remains relevant today. As such, it would be no surprise if the tactic was being used amid the growing U.S.-China competition over AI and advanced semiconductors.

“Meiren ji” is one of “ Thirty-Six Stratagems ,” a Chinese military text of uncertain origin but generally believed to have derived from oral and written histories from the Warring States period — 475–221 BCE. Its 31st stratagem states that personal relationships can be used to influence political opponents and recommends exploiting an adversary’s personal desires and emotional vulnerabilities to weaken their judgment and undermine their leadership.
The “Thirty-Six Stratagems” is both a playbook for warfare and a reflection on past experience.
Indeed, one of China’s most famous beauty stratagem stories dates back more than 2,000 years to the Spring and Autumn period of Chinese history.

In the fifth century BCE, King Goujian of Yue, in modern-day southern China, was defeated by King Fuchai of Wu, its northern neighbor, and forced to submit. But Goujian secretly rebuilt his strength and prepared for revenge.
According to the ancient historical text “ Wu Yue Chun Qiu ,” Yue sent two beautiful women – Xi Shi and Zheng Dan – to Fuchai, hoping he would become distracted by pleasure and neglect state affairs.
The plan reportedly worked. Fuchai, seemingly enchanted by the beautiful women, gradually ignored Yue’s threat. Meanwhile, Goujian prepared for war and in 473 BCE Yue conquered Wu.
Xi Shi’s actual role in Wu’s downfall remains unclear. Wu’s defeat involved poor political decisions and Yue’s military recovery.
Still, the story illustrated an important idea in Chinese political strategy: Eexploiting an opponent’s personal weaknesses can sometimes be more effective than confronting him directly.
A similar tactic appears in the 14th-century novel “ Romance of the Three Kingdoms ,” considered one of the classics of Chinese literature.

It tells the story of Dong Zhuo, a powerful warlord who controlled the imperial court during the late Eastern Han Dynasty. To remove him, Wang Yun, a senior court official loyal to the Han Dynasty promised a beautiful young woman, named Diaochan, in marriage to Dong Zhuo’s military commander. He then offered the same woman to Dong Zhuo.

The scheme fueled jealousy and distrust between the two men, eventually enabling Wang Yun to persuade Dong Zhuo’s underling to kill him. Wang Yun then briefly took charge of the imperial court on behalf of the Han emperor.

In modern intelligence operations, using romantic or sexual relationships to approach targets, obtain sensitive information or exert influence is commonly called a “ honey trap .” It is, moreover, certainly not unique to China. Western and Soviet intelligence agencies used intimate relationships for espionage frequently during the Cold War .

Modern China also has documented cases. One example involves French diplomat Bernard Boursicot and the Chinese opera performer Shi Pei Pu . The pair met in Beijing in 1964 and maintained a long-term intimate relationship. Throughout, Boursicot was providing French diplomatic documents to China. The spying was eventually exposed and both involved were prosecuted for espionage in France in the 1980s.

A more recent example involves former U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell and Christine Fang , a suspected Chinese intelligence operative. Swalwell acknowledged in 2015 that he had been physically intimate with Fang on several occasions. At the time, Fang helped raise funds for Swalwell’s campaign and helped place an intern in his congressional office.

Jensen Huang’s position would make him a prime target for such a “honey trap” operation. His company has become central to the technological competition between the U.S and China. As AI becomes increasingly important to economic development, military capabilities and national security, moreover, Washington has repeatedly tightened restrictions on advanced AI chip exports to China, hoping to slow its access to computing power.
Beijing is investing heavily in domestic semiconductor development . Yet Chinese companies still need advanced chips to train AI models and build data centers.
From Beijing’s perspective , advanced AI chips matter not only for Chinese technology companies but for future military and technological competition.
This puts Nvidia in a particularly important position and helps explain the national security concerns surrounding Huang.

However, strategic motives do not prove an intelligence operation occurred. Jensen Huang’s importance does not, in itself, establish that he was targeted by a honey trap or that Alice Huang acted for Chinese intelligence. Those are allegations that still require full investigation.

Yet it is surely true that in modern politics – just as in ancient China’s rivalries – rivals seek information about opponents, try to influence important decisions and exploit weaknesses to gain strategic advantages.
What has changed is who controls important strategic resources.

In ancient China, influencing a ruler through personal relationships could affect a country’s political and military decisions. Today, approaching a major technology executive could offer access to sensitive technologies.
More than 2,000 years ago, a powerful state could lose its advantage through a ruler’s personal weaknesses. Today, political and technological power are distributed differently.
But as long as important decisions depend on individuals, personal relationships may remain a weakness that rivals can exploit.

articles.title: Far from farms and cities, dry climates are boosting river nitrate pollution
articles.author:
<name>Li Li (李黎), Professor of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Penn State</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/li-li-1470183"/>
paras: Typically, when people hear about nitrates, it involves runoff from farm fields, sewage systems and cities that can fuel harmful algae blooms and raise the risk of a serious illness in infants known as “ blue baby syndrome .”

But a river can also run through a sparsely populated landscape with little farming and still contain surprisingly high levels of this form of nitrogen that can harm aquatic life, drinking water and human health.

In a new study, my colleague and I found a reason why that happens: Dry climate conditions are associated with high river nitrate concentrations , even in places with little farming or urban development.

We found nitrate hot spots in some unexpected places, including the Rocky Mountains of the western United States and northern Africa’s Sahara Desert. Where water is scarce, we found that nitrates – which can naturally leach into surface water and groundwater from the soil as microbes break down organic material – were able to accumulate and become concentrated rather than being diluted or flushed away.

That raises health concerns for regions where nitrates in rivers and well water might not be given much thought. It also raises questions about how nitrate-related health risks will increase as global temperatures rise.

To see how widespread this pattern is, we combined global measurements from more than 7,000 monitoring sites and additionally extracted information about climate, soils, land use and other landscape features. We then trained machine learning models to estimate long-term average nitrate concentrations across nearly 2.9 million river segments worldwide.
The resulting map suggests that nitrates deserve attention well beyond the urban and agricultural regions where they are usually monitored.

High nitrate exposure in water and food is particularly dangerous for infants because it can interfere with the blood’s ability to carry oxygen. Blue baby syndrome , or methemoglobinemia, can result in serious illnesses and be caused by nitrate poisoning.
The U.S. drinking water standard of 10 milligrams of nitrate-nitrogen per liter was established primarily to guard against this acute risk.
We estimate that about 37,000 people worldwide live in areas where rivers exceed the 10 mg/L drinking water standard, predominantly in the U.S. Corn Belt.

That doesn’t mean 37,000 people are drinking water at those concentrations, since river water in many regions is treated before it is supplied for drinking. But it’s a concerning level they should be aware of, particularly those using well water .

Research has also raised concerns about possible effects of long-term exposure to nitrate at lower concentrations, including certain cancers and adverse birth outcomes , such as babies born preterm or with a low birth weight, although those risks are still being studied.
We estimate that about 480 million people worldwide live in areas where nearby rivers have elevated long-term average nitrate concentrations, above 2.5 milligrams per liter.

Many of the rivers our models identified as having elevated nitrate levels are small headwater streams. Many headwater streams cease to flow for some periods of time every year, and nitrates can accumulate to high concentrations under dry or low-flow conditions. These small streams make up most of the global river networks , have long been overlooked and feed larger rivers that supply drinking water to large populations and help shape the quality of water downstream.
Too much nitrate in rivers and lakes can also fuel algal growth and disrupt aquatic ecosystems.

A global map of nitrate concentrations in river water cannot show what comes out of someone’s tap. Their water may be mixed with other sources or treated before they drink it . Nitrate concentrations can also rise and fall over time, while our map shows long-term averages.
To understand a person’s actual exposure will require connecting river measurements with drinking water sources, treatment practices and tests of water delivered to households.

Many rivers with nitrate concentrations above 2.5 milligrams per liter flow through sparsely populated regions where access to treated drinking water may be limited. Even where treatment facilities exist, conventional methods remove little nitrate . Removing it requires specialized technologies that can be costly to operate.

Our study shows why more drylands and small headwater streams need to be monitored for nitrate. It also raises a question for a warming world: If a region becomes drier, how much will nitrate concentrations rise even if people do not add more nitrogen to the landscape?

Answering that will require measurements through wet and dry periods, paired with studies of how water moves through soils, groundwater and rivers. For now, the message is clear: Protecting water quality requires paying attention to the climate as well as to the human activities that put nitrogen into the environment.

      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/meagen-rosenthal-1041364"/>
paras: Mountains of scientific evidence support both the negative and positive effects of our eating habits on our health . Research shows that a healthy diet can help those suffering from chronic health conditions like Type 2 diabetes , heart disease and high blood pressure .

This is where “food is medicine” comes in. Food is medicine, also known as “food as medicine” and “food prescriptions,” is a movement dedicated to providing healthy food – fruits, vegetables and sometimes healthy proteins – based on a clinician’s prescription in order to prevent, manage or treat specific clinical conditions .
Prescribing food to patients is intended to convey that food is just as important as medication for health and wellness.

As researchers whose work focuses on food access and health in rural communities, we have firsthand experience running food is medicine programs in our local area in northern Mississippi. This experience has shown us the benefits and limitations of these programs in our community.

Food is medicine programs can be delivered through curated food boxes, grocery vouchers and medically tailored meals. Most programs are collaborations between nonprofit organizations, health clinics and healthcare providers. The goal of food is medicine is to improve patient health, especially for those with chronic conditions, while reducing healthcare costs.

Increasingly, food is medicine programs have become lifelines for people with food insecurity. In 2024, more than 47 million Americans, including 7.3 million children, lived in food-insecure households – meaning they were at some point uncertain of having, or did not have, enough food for everyone in the household.

Internationally, the number of people experiencing hunger rises to roughly 673 million . Rural populations are more likely to be food insecure due to the loss of local grocery stores and distance from urban centers. Unlike a food bank, food is medicine programs provide only healthy foods, which are often curated by a dietitian, to optimize patient health.

Though food is medicine isn’t formally connected to the Make American Healthy Again movement , U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. has brought new energy and attention to the concept. In January 2026, the second Trump administration launched a campaign encouraging Americans to “ Eat Real Food .”

But the food is medicine movement actually began more than 60 years ago. One of the early providers who prescribed food as medicine was civil rights activist and multiple Nobel Peace Prize winner Dr. Jack Geiger . In the 1960s, he co-founded community health centers in South Boston and the Mississippi Delta.
When government officials chastised him for prescribing food to patients in the Delta, Geiger responded, “The last time I looked at my textbooks, the most specific therapy for malnutrition was food.”
Since then, thousands of community organizations like Community Servings and Project Open Hand have provided healthy food to vulnerable community members.

In 2023, the president of the American Heart Association convened an advisory group of researchers and physicians to review current food is medicine research and suggest next steps for work in this area. This advisory has suggested that these programs could help prevent or manage chronic conditions, saving the U.S. healthcare system an estimated US$4.3 trillion annually .

Food is medicine has also started to gain international momentum. In 2025, the Rockefeller Foundation supported a meeting of international scholars, policy experts and practitioners that established the Food Is Medicine Global Alliance . This organization plans to help integrate, sustainably finance and routinely deliver food is medicine programs worldwide by 2030. So far, it has released several reports highlighting the current food is medicine environment and made resources available to providers looking to start their own programs.

Food is medicine programs can use food from local farms or grocery stores, and the means of getting the food to patients varies. The four projects we have run to date have been relatively small and local.

One was a food box pickup program that supplemented fruits and vegetables for 55 households whose members demonstrated food insecurity. We followed the participants for two years and found statistically significant reductions in weight , waist circumference and triglyceride levels in the primary adult participants.

For two of our other programs, including one that is ongoing, we partnered with local farmers . One was a pilot test of a food box delivery program for housebound people. Both the recipients of the food and the farmers reported high satisfaction with the program’s delivery and felt the program strengthened community connections while also supporting local agricultural livelihoods.
One recent large-scale literature review identified 14 trials of food is medicine interventions and found that these approaches often positively influenced diet quality and food security .

Another review of food is medicine programs for people with diabetes found significant increases in fruit and vegetable intake and reductions in blood sugar levels . This data supports our own previous findings.

However, the effect of food is medicine programs on long-term health outcomes has been inconsistent, in part because many trials have been too small or not rigorous enough to determine causation. In some cases, the “dose” – that is, the amount of food provided – is limited by grant funding. Our food box pickup project supplemented only four to five meals each week , which may have been insufficient to significantly improve all health outcomes.

Moreover, it will be important for researchers to consider the logistics of making these programs work in various local food environments. Global factors like changing weather patterns and, more recently, delays in fuel and supplies from the Strait of Hormuz have increased prices of staple food products like cereals and vegetable oil and led to shortages of cooking oil in some countries.

Food is medicine can be appealing because it makes intuitive sense. But going forward, larger, high-quality studies are needed to adequately track clinical outcomes from the various types of food is medicine programming. If studies show food is medicine is beneficial, it could lead to a shift in how healthcare practitioners approach diet for patients with chronic illness. Access to healthy food would be considered as essential as medications for patients with chronic illness.

articles.title: Extreme weather risk is scaring big corporations away from poorer countries – that hurts the companies, too
articles.author:
<name>Jonas Gamso, Associate Professor of International Trade and Global Studies, Arizona State University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/jonas-gamso-511800"/>
paras: When multinational companies decide where to build a factory, open a mine or establish a regional office, they have to consider whether the investment will still be profitable years into the future.

Making that decision increasingly means thinking about risks, like whether surrounding roads will flood, worker safety will be compromised by extreme heat in the summer, and clean water will be available.

As climate change increases the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events around the world, these effects can be especially severe in poorer countries that lack the resources to prepare for disasters or recover quickly after they hit.

I study how political and environmental risks affect international business . In my new book, “ Multinational Corporations and Climate Change: Risks, Responsibilities, and Resilience ,” I explore how disaster risk is affecting the ways global companies see these climate-vulnerable markets, and how those views are leading some foreign investors to avoid these developing nations altogether.

Low- and middle-income countries aren’t the only ones that suffer when multinational corporations pass them by. The companies themselves also stand to lose out on business opportunities in emerging markets if they pull away.

Evidence from several studies suggests that multinationals are systematically avoiding investing in the most climate-vulnerable countries. These include my own analysis of 159 countries. Although these studies focus on different samples, they identify the same trend: Countries characterized by greater climate vulnerability received less foreign investment .

The results are not trivial. My book identifies a 12% reduction in foreign direct investment for each 1-point rise in climate vulnerability on a 100-point scale, while holding other relevant factors constant. This vulnerability data measures countries’ exposure to climate hazards as well as their capacity to adapt.
Companies rarely say why they’re avoiding a particular location, but their climate-related concerns occasionally become visible.

For example, Google halted plans to build a US$200 million data center in Chile after an environmental court revoked its construction permit over the likely effects on water supplies and the environment. Similarly, a $1 billion data center proposed in Kenya by Microsoft and the Abu Dhabi-based artificial intelligence company G42 was delayed and ultimately suspended amid concerns about water stress in the area.
Companies have reason to be cautious about climate risks.

One analysis of 71 large publicly traded companies found that firms reporting major flood losses experienced a 5% average decline in shareholder value over the following year, after accounting for broader market movements.
In Vietnam, typhoons and floods caused an estimated $475 million in damage to energy and transportation infrastructure in 2022. Unreliable infrastructure cost companies there about $280 million .

Severe flooding in Thailand in 2011 forced several companies, including Toyota, Nissan and Honda, to temporarily suspend production as factories flooded, shutting down production of parts or vehicles made there.
Costs like those shape where companies choose to invest next.

While climate risk does not stop all investment in climate-vulnerable markets, it does make projects in these nations relatively more expensive, less attractive and more difficult to finance than less risky locations.

For developing countries, less foreign investment means fewer jobs are created . These countries also have fewer opportunities to benefit from exposure to the new technologies that multinationals bring when they invest abroad.

Those results highlight another way climate change is deepening global inequality. It reduces the economic activity that could support future development, while simultaneously damaging physical infrastructure and threatening human health and well-being.

Developing countries are especially vulnerable to the effects of rising global temperatures, whether for their dependence on agricultural markets, geography or relatively fragile infrastructure . A report from the Climate Impact Lab at the University of Chicago projects that 90% of heat-related deaths in the coming decades will take place in low- and middle-income countries. Similarly, a 2022 study found that around 90% of people exposed to flooding live in developing nations.

Yet poor countries have contributed only a tiny fraction of the emissions that are causing climate change, even as they face the brunt of the damage. For example, African countries are responsible for less than 4% of greenhouse gas emissions globally. But they stand to experience the greatest negative effects of climate change.
When a company avoids investing in climate-vulnerable countries, that may reduce its exposure to floods, droughts or extreme heat, but the decision also carries potential costs for the company.

Many of these countries have growing consumer markets, energy resources or critical minerals that multinationals need. Companies that dismiss them as too risky may lose out on promising opportunities.

For example, the Democratic Republic of Congo supplies most of the world’s cobalt , while Indonesia has become the dominant producer of nickel . These countries are highly vulnerable to climate change , which is likely scaring some companies away .

Yet companies with a greater tolerance for risk have established strong positions in those countries’ mineral industries . Thus, more cautious firms may reduce their risk exposure, but they are also surrendering access to important resources and growing markets.
There are ways to help companies overcome their climate-risk avoidance so more investment can pour into these countries:

Foreign aid from wealthy countries can help developing countries shore up their roads, ports, electrical grids and water systems before extreme storms or droughts occur. My 2025 study found that climate-vulnerable countries that received more aid for climate adaptation also received more foreign direct investment than those receiving less aid. The result suggests the funding may reassure companies that climate risks are being addressed.

International development banks can share some of the risks by providing climate risk insurance to multinationals. This would offer a safety net to absorb some of the losses if a covered disruption prevents a project from operating as intended. The World Bank already offers similar coverage against political risk incidents, which has given companies confidence to invest in countries such as Kenya , Mozambique and Nigeria .

Better data can give companies more precise information about climate risks. Many risk scores label entire nations as vulnerable or not, even though exposure varies from one city or project site to another. More detailed information about local flood exposure, water availability, heat, infrastructure and adaptation capabilities would allow companies to limit their avoidance to the riskiest areas, instead of bypassing those countries altogether.

Understanding the local risk, insuring companies against risk and helping countries make their infrastructure more resilient to storms, droughts and heat can help boost investment in ways that benefit the companies and spur economic growth and development in climate-vulnerable countries at the same time.

articles.title: Despite intense Islamophobia, Abdul El-Sayed and dozens of other Muslims elected representatives are breaking down barriers
articles.author:
<name>Nazita Lajevardi, Associate Professor of Political Science, University of Michigan</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/nazita-lajevardi-2776389"/>
paras: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed made history on Nov. 3, 2026, when Michigan voters elected him the first Muslim to the U.S. Senate despite significant efforts to defeat him.
He wasn’t alone. A record number of American Muslims won their races in the midterms.

As political scientists who study minority politics, we think their wins raise a question that goes beyond any single race: What does it mean for Muslim Americans, and for everyone else, to see Muslims elected to public office?

The August 2026 Democratic primary alone drew record-breaking outside spending from the pro-Israel lobbying group AIPAC and corporate special interests, totaling nearly US$70 million to defeat El-Sayed. That is about 11 times his own spending.

In the November 2026 midterm election, outside groups, including super PACs and other organizations independent of the campaigns, spent more than $134 million, according to independent trackers . The largest spender was the Senate Leadership Fund, a super PAC aligned with some Senate Republican leaders .

El-Sayed also broke with his party’s leadership on Gaza. As a candidate, he called for ending U.S. arms sales to Israel and opposed what he called “ blank-check military aid ” to any foreign country. That stance resonated with the many Arab and Muslim Americans who had split with Democrats over the war in 2024.

El-Sayed also faced a barrage of openly Islamophobic attacks expressing hatred or hostility toward Islam or Muslims. President Donald Trump called him a “ jihadist ” and a “Muslim Brotherhood guy.” Vice President JD Vance accused him of supporting Sharia law . And in the week after El-Sayed’s primary win, anti-Muslim posts targeting him online rose about twentyfold .
El-Sayed won anyway. Across the country, at least 97 American Muslims won federal, state and local races this year, according to the Council on American-Islamic Relations.
Political scientists have long studied descriptive representation – the election of politicians who share the background of the people they serve, such as their race, ethnicity, gender or religion.

One of the earliest studies came from sociologist Lawrence Bobo and political scientist Franklin Gilliam Jr. , who found that Black Americans living in cities with a Black mayor were more politically engaged than Black Americans elsewhere. Those who resided in cities with a Black mayor were more likely to report being trusting of government, more confident that they could make a difference and more attentive to politics.

Later scholars called this the “minority empowerment thesis,” meaning that when members of a minority group are elected, other members of that group feel more connected to politics. For example, political scientists Susan A. Banducci , Todd Donovan and Jeffrey A. Karp found that Black Americans represented by a Black member of Congress were significantly more likely than other Black Americans to know their representative’s name. They were also more likely to have contacted their representative and to remember something they had done for the district.
For Muslim Americans, the stakes are especially high because research shows that, at times, hostility pushes them away from public life.

During the 2016 presidential campaign, Trump called for “ a total and complete shutdown of Muslims entering the United States .” Around that time, users of the social media platform X, then known as Twitter, who had Arabic names shared their locations 10% to 20% less often . It was a sign that they were making themselves less visible online. In the same study, Muslim Americans surveyed in early 2017 who reported experiencing societal discrimination also indicated avoiding public places – such as restaurants, shopping malls and parks – and limiting what they posted online.

Political scientist Nura Sediqe has studied what social psychologist Elizabeth Pinel called “ stigma consciousness ”: expecting to be judged and treated differently because of a part of one’s identity that others look down on. In a survey of Muslims in southeast Michigan, Sediqe found that the more strongly they expected this, the less likely they were to identify as American. That expectation was highest among those who had faced discrimination and among women who wear the hijab, a headscarf that is a visible marker of their faith. In other words, being made to feel like an outsider can weaken Muslims’ sense that they belong in the country, and in its democracy.

Muslims also face barriers from elected officials of both parties. In an audit study of state legislators in all 50 states, for example, both Democrats and Republicans were less likely to respond to a Muslim constituent than a white one.

To understand what visible Muslim representation can change, we conducted two experiments in May 2022. We created a one-minute animated video showing “a day in the life of a city council member,” designed to resemble the short explainer videos that companies and government agencies use online to explain their work to the public.

Survey respondents were randomly assigned to watch one of two versions. In one, three council members were visibly Muslim. In the other, the same three characters appeared without religious symbols. Because the videos were otherwise identical, any differences in how people responded can be attributed to seeing Muslims on the council. The first study surveyed 740 American Muslims, and the second nearly 4,000 non-Muslim Americans.

In both studies, people who saw the council with visibly Muslim members judged it to be fairer and more legitimate. The effect was strongest among Muslims, but non-Muslims rated the council slightly fairer and more legitimate, too.

Muslim participants who saw visibly Muslim leaders were also more willing to take part in politics. On average, they were about 5 percentage points more likely to say they planned to do things like contact a public official, attend a local political meeting or join a protest in the coming year. They also showed a small increase in interest in running for office.

Our research suggests that representation is not zero-sum, meaning that making a political body more inclusive for one group did not come at the expense of another. That challenges a common worry that elevating one group will alienate everyone else. Readers should note that we used short animated videos of a fictional city council, not real elected officials, so more research is needed to know how these effects play out with real politicians and how long they last.

Still, these findings do matter in a moment like this one. During the campaign, Representative Nancy Mace of South Carolina posted that “every single Muslim holding public office in America is a Trojan horse and a threat to both national security and our republic.”
But our research points the other way. Seeing Muslims in office made both Muslims and non-Muslims alike view a political body as fairer and more legitimate.

We argue that El-Sayed’s presence in the Senate, alongside the record number of Muslims elected across the country, has the potential to not only show Muslim Americans that they belong in American democracy, but also to show everyone else that the country’s institutions are stronger for it.

articles.title: Rural women in Colorado and nationwide are at higher risk for cervical cancer – at-home test kits can help close the gap
articles.author:
<name>Christine Conageski, Professor of Obstetrics and Gynecology, University of Colorado Anschutz</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/christine-conageski-2768071"/>
paras: With vaccines and regular screening, cervical cancer is one of the most preventable cancers.
Yet women living in rural areas of the United States have a 25% higher rate of cervical cancer – and a 42% higher rate of death from the disease compared to urban women.
In Colorado, rural counties such as Prowers, Moffat and Montrose have almost three times the rate of cervical cancer than urban counties .

Nationwide, 13,000 women are diagnosed with the disease and more than 4,000 die from it each year . In Colorado, the most recent data available indicated that almost 150 women were diagnosed with cervical cancer in 2023 , and, on average, more than 40 women die annually .

While overall numbers of diagnoses and deaths nationwide have decreased over the past 20 years, rural women are more likely to be diagnosed at a later stage of disease , meaning chemotherapy and radiation treatments may be necessary to treat their disease.

My research and clinical expertise in gynecology and obstetrics specifically aim to tackle this troubling health disparity. I study lower genital tract precancers from human papillomavirus, or HPV. As part of a team of researchers across the U.S., I participated in a clinical trial that led to the first FDA-approved at-home HPV test.

The development of an at-home test is a game changer. It can bring screening to a broader spectrum of women, hopefully catching those who have precancerous changes early enough to prevent the progression to cancer.
But eliminating cervical cancer will require ensuring that women can access not only screening but also vaccines and any necessary follow-up diagnostic procedures and treatments.

For rural women, access to healthcare clinics for routine screenings may be limited. A visit to a qualified professional for a cervical exam and Pap test can require half a day or longer in travel and wait times. In a recent study, women in rural counties were 20% less likely to be up to date on cervical cancer screening .

In 2025, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration authorized the Teal Wand for at-home self-collection . Federal and medical organizations have since included self-collection as part of routine screening recommendations. My university received funding from Teal Health to support research. I was a site investigator, but I have no shares in the company or any patents, and I have never received any money directly from Teal.
Women can now also do a test during a visit to their primary care doctor even if that doctor does not perform pelvic exams. That means patients do not need to see a gynecologist to get screened.

Nearly all cervical cancers are caused by persistent viral infections from HPV. These infections most frequently occur through sexual contact. At-home screening tests check for infection, which means clinicians can identify women at risk of developing cervical cancer before the disease occurs.
During self-collection, women use a simple swab to collect a vaginal sample. That swab is mailed to the lab and then tested for HPV.
Studies have shown that when FDA-approved HPV tests are used, self-collected samples are as reliable as clinician-collected samples for detecting cervical precancer.

Studies show that self-collection tests for HPV can help decrease barriers to care for rural communities. A study across four Appalachian state regions – Ohio, West Virginia, Kentucky and Virginia – found that screening increases when women are mailed a self-collection kit . Appalachia, a largely rural geographic region that is underserved in terms of access to healthcare, has documented disparities in cervical cancer rates.

Underscreened patients across these four states were randomly chosen to either receive the usual care, a mailed reminder letter to go to a clinic or a mailed HPV self-collection kit. The study showed a threefold increase in screening rates: 5% with the reminder and 15% with the mailed kits.
Another study in Washington state showed similar results, with an increase in screening of overdue individuals by more than 15% in mailed kits versus education alone .

Statewide initiatives in Alabama, with the Operation Wipe Out project , and in Texas, with the Lone Star Cervical Cancer Elimination Plan , use self-screening as part of a strategy to eliminate cervical cancer.
In Colorado, I am part of a team working to implement a similar plan that we hope to initiate in 2027.

Studies in Europe have shown that self-collection has increased access to care, improved screening rates and reduced screening costs. Long-term evidence demonstrates these programs are effective: Many countries began using them as early as 2017.

Making screening easier is only the first step toward preventing cervical cancer. Even in the Appalachian study, fewer than 15 out of 100 women who received mailed HPV self-collection kits completed screening .
In short, removing the need for a clinic visit does not address all the barriers to preventing this disease.

HPV vaccines are the single strongest tool for preventing cervical cancer . Vaccinations are recommended for adolescents ages 9-14 before they are exposed to HPV. If given under age 15, two shots six months apart are required. No booster is needed. Individuals who do not receive the vaccine before turning 15 can get a “catch-up” vaccine as a three-shot series up to age 45.

For women who test positive for high-risk HPV, additional testing may be necessary to identify precancerous changes in the cervix. In rural communities, accessing these services can be even more challenging than obtaining screening.

Mobile clinics can bring services closer to patients. Training more clinicians to provide colposcopy services could improve access to diagnostic care. Colposcopy is an exam in which a healthcare provider uses a lighted magnifying instrument to look closely at the cervix for abnormal or precancerous changes. A small tissue sample may be taken for diagnostic testing.

Patient navigators and community health workers can also assist women in overcoming barriers to care. A patient navigator is a trained professional who helps overcome roadblocks by providing education, coordinating services, connecting patients with resources and supporting them through the healthcare system to ensure timely access to care.
Rural women in Colorado and elsewhere urgently need a concerted effort from statewide programs and health centers to decrease the incidence and deaths from this disease.
Christine Conageski received research funding from Teal Health, Inc. She is affiliated with the American Society for Colposcopy and Cervical Pathology (ASCCP).

articles.title: Wilson Greenlights Expansion of Surveillance in Seattle
articles.author: Amy Sundberg
paras: On Tuesday, Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson announced that the City will be immediately moving forward with the expansion of the Seattle Police Department’s (SPD’s) surveillance program that was approved by city council last fall.

To assist her in this decision, Wilson engaged the New York University (NYU) Policing Project to perform a governance audit assessing the civil rights and liberties risks posed by SPD’s surveillance program, including their real-time crime center, CCTV cameras, and Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) cameras. Wilson said the City plans to implement many of the recommendations outlined in the report.
NYU didn’t assess the civil liberties risks of Seattle’s automated license plate readers due to their usage being suspended earlier in the year to comply with a new state law .

During her campaign, Wilson ran on an anti-surveillance platform, and at the beginning of her term, activists asked her to turn off all of SPD’s surveillance cameras. Instead, Wilson opted to postpone the installation of new SPD cameras in two new areas: the Capitol Hill nightlife district and an area around Garfield High School in the Central District. Wilson allowed new cameras to be installed in the Stadium District but only turned them on while Seattle was hosting World Cup matches this summer.
The NYU audit appears to have satisfied any qualms Wilson had about increasing the surveillance apparatus in Seattle.

“When I paused the expansion of CCTV, I did so because I believed we needed to ask some hard questions about data security and the protection of civil liberties, especially in the context of a federal administration that is targeting vulnerable communities and violating civil rights,” said Wilson. “After reviewing the evidence, the recommendations, and the safeguards available to us, I believe there is an important and responsible role for the RTCC within Seattle's public-safety system.”
The NYU Policing Project did not conduct any analysis around the cybersecurity risks of the data being collected by SPD.

Wilson said that Seattle has fewer surveillance cameras (so far) than many other American cities, an observation that hits differently at a time when the U.S. government is ramping up mass surveillance and the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is planning to deploy a domestic surveillance program in Seattle early next year.

Nevertheless, the surveillance cameras in the Stadium District will be turned back on immediately, and the City will proceed with the plans to procure and install cameras in the Capitol Hill nightlife district and the Central District.

“I also want to emphasize that these are not Flock cameras,” Wilson said. “Our system is managed by a company called Axon, and while there are obviously similarities in the technology, I think it's fair to say that Axon has a more responsive record.”

While less widely criticized than Flock, Axon has been receiving plenty of negative attention in its own right. In 2025 alone, Axon held $31.9 million in contracts with the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). And just last week, a class action lawsuit was brought against Axon, alleging that Axon “blatantly violated” rules enacted by the California State Legislature regarding how Axon can capture, use, and store the data collected by their license plate readers.

“Like its competitors, Axon sells a centralized, vendor-controlled camera system that municipalities rent,” said Noah Williams, a local cybersecurity expert and member of advocacy group Communities Not Cameras. “Unlike Flock, it provides municipalities with a false sense of control over their camera footage.”

Wilson’s change of heart came in spite of the NYU audit clearly stating that SPD’s real-time crime center does involve real civil liberties risks. “Short of ceasing to retain RTCC data altogether, SPD cannot eliminate fully the risk that such data could be obtained and used for purposes prohibited under Washington law,” the report reads.
Vulnerabilities include data obtained via public disclosure laws, data obtained via subpoena of either the City or Axon, and data obtained illegally.

The City of Seattle paid the NYU Policing Project $223,000 for the audit, which found the same kind of sloppiness, lack of clear policies, and failure to live up to commitments in SPD’s surveillance program that were highlighted in the recent audits by the Seattle Office of the Auditor and the other from the Office of the Inspector General (OIG).

The original SPD surveillance pilot installed cameras in the Third Street corridor downtown, the Chinatown-International District (CID), and Aurora Avenue in North Seattle. Since that time, SPD has been given access to a large number of SDOT traffic safety cameras through their real-time crime center, as well as incorporating 23 private cameras from three private businesses, all of which are located in the Capitol Hill nightlife district where Wilson had said she was pausing SPD camera surveillance.
The private cameras in Capitol Hill were plugged into SPD’s real-time crime center with no notice to community members.

Ryan Talen, a nurse who lives in Capitol Hill and member of Communities Not Cameras, was unaware of the private cameras in his neighborhood being streamed into SPD’s real-time crime center until The Urbanist let him know after the press conference.
“It's a violation of our privacy,” Talen told The Urbanist .

The University of Pennsylvania is performing a separate audit in cooperation with the OIG, initiated during Mayor Bruce Harrell’s term, on the efficacy of SPD’s surveillance program. According to the NYU audit, the University of Pennsylvania’s audit won’t be completed until late next year.
Not everyone found the NYU audit as reassuring as Wilson.

“The report revealed what we've known since visiting the RTCC,” Communities Not Cameras said in a statement. “The recommendations to reform the RTCC in the report are half-measures. More oversight, audit policies and targeted use won't eliminate the fact that this system can and will be abused. Seattle has had a long history of police brutality and corruption and a short history of community healing. We need more of the latter. Addressing poverty, mental health and solving root causes of crime is what will make us safer.”

The NYU audit was conducted by a team of lawyers who found that there are “significant gaps” in the governance around the real-time crime center and made 19 recommendations that the authors say should be implemented if SPD continues their surveillance program.

The audit’s purpose was not to call out the general benefits and risks of SPD’s use of the real-time crime center, nor to make a recommendation on whether SPD’s surveillance should continue as designed.

However, in an apparent contradiction to Wilson’s claims that adding more surveillance cameras to SPD’s real-time crime center will make Seattle “safer,” the audit states, “Although the potential benefits of the RTCC as described by the City are plausible, the current research base supporting these benefits is thin. There is more robust research studying the public safety impacts of CCTVs on their own (i.e., not connected to an RTCC), but that research is best characterized as mixed.”

At the press conference, Wilson appeared to be focused more on the potential upsides of surveillance, albeit not currently backed by empirical studies, as opposed to the costs of expanding a technology that is known to aid in repression and authoritarian control.
“Once data exists, no city or agency can guarantee it will never be shared,” the audit emphasized.

According to the audit, there is an important distinction between targeted surveillance and what a real-time crime center does, which is categorized as “indiscriminate surveillance,” meaning the system surveils the public at large and collects information about people who are not suspected of any offense or wrongdoing. Indeed, due to the real-time crime center integrating many different technologies, the audit says, “The centralization of surveillance systems and data can enable far more powerful and intrusive forms of surveillance than any one system could accomplish on its own.”

When considering the many gaps, lack of clear policy, and lack of follow-through outlined in the audit, it’s striking that SPD had an entire two years since council approval of the real-time crime center surveillance pilot to make progress on these goals. The real-time crime center became operational on May 20, 2025 . Thus, the City has been operating this surveillance system for almost a year and a half without the development of basic policies for its use and the timely delivery of commitments SPD made as part of the City’s Surveillance Impact Review process. This lack of engaging seriously with the agreements and responsibilities around using such a robust surveillance apparatus seems in line with SPD’s past conduct regarding surveillance technologies in the City.

Auditors found that there is a lack of clarity around the approved purpose of SPD’s real-time crime center, centering on whether it should be used for low-level misdemeanors as well as more serious incidents. According to the report, SPD found guidance that limited surveillance use for misdemeanors “challenging from an operational perspective,” and yet the surveillance pilot was originally passed with the intention of reducing gun violence and human trafficking (despite no empirical evidence has proven that this kind of surveillance reduces either of these categories of crime).

In practice, the City is left with a surveillance system that could theoretically be used to police low-level issues like trespassing, public drug use, or shoplifting a package of diapers. Wilson refused to comment on this possibility other than to state that she’s looking forward to the University of Pennsylvania report that she expects to provide information as to how the real-time crime center is being used. Wilson’s answer suggests that the Mayor’s Office doesn’t expect to fully understand how SPD is using its surveillance system until two and a half years after it went operational.

While “real-time” is in the name, in practice the crime center is also used after the fact to investigate past events. If surveillance footage were to be used by SPD after the fact to track someone without a warrant, this usage would raise constitutional concerns and could potentially land the City in legal hot water. However, Wilson said SPD does not currently use the center for this purpose.

In addition, there are no firm policies in place for how to use the real-time crime center for large events. While passive monitoring of SPD camera feeds appears to be prohibited by policy, in practice, the auditors discovered that SPD created a case number for the entire World Cup and streamed live camera feeds through the real-time crime center throughout World Cup events.

Surveillance at protests is another gray area of SPD’s surveillance program, and the audit recommends SPD develop policies around the real-time crime center and protest activities that are protected by the First Amendment. Currently, demonstrations are captured by default if they take place where SPD and SDOT cameras are installed.

In order to improve transparency, the audit recommended that SPD fulfill its two outstanding Surveillance Impact Review commitments made in 2024: to have a public-facing dashboard that reports on real-time crime center use and to develop “an omnibus surveillance technology policy.” SPD told researchers that both projects were delayed but in process, and Wilson announced at the press conference that both projects would be completed. Why SPD would need an outside agency like the NYU Policing Project to recommend they fulfill their own previous commitments remains unclear.

“It's disappointing how unscientific this whole process is,” Ryan Talen, a nurse at Harborview and member of Communities Not Cameras, told The Urbanist . “It doesn't even feel like there are standards. You know, we're just accepting the SPD's word after they say they're going to do something, they're not doing it, and we're still moving forward with the program. What does that tell us about who's calling the shots around here? Clearly, not the people that elected Katie Wilson.”

The auditors also recommended SPD institute a five-day data retention policy, given that’s what SPD say they already do in practice, and that they institute a data retention policy around the data they clip and attach to investigations so they don’t retain the data indefinitely, long after a particular investigation is closed.

“Video clips and other data stored on Evidence.com are retained by SPD indefinitely, resulting in a substantial and growing repository of data that outside agencies could seek to obtain,” the report reads. Evidence.com is Axon’s cloud-based evidence management system.

Another recommendation suggests that SPD should publish “in a clear and conspicuous location on its website” a full list of the tools and features it is using — and seeking approval to use — in its real-time crime center at least twice a year, as well as institute a policy for regular internal audits of the real-time crime center. In addition to internal audits, NYU researchers suggested the OIG should add identifying material changes to SPD’s use of surveillance tools to its annual audit requirements.

What the audit fails to address is what to do if SPD fails to implement these recommendations in practice. The OIG audit from October, for example, showed that SPD has already failed in its commitment to make sure every camera has privacy masking in place if it’s facing a private residence. And SPD has failed to live up to commitments it made in the Surveillance Impact Review back in 2024, even though two years have passed.

articles.title: Latest Look at 'Tactical Urbanism' Planned for Stadium District
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: A street transformation is coming to the Stadium District's front porch, with plans advancing for " tactical urbanism " along Occidental Avenue South near Lumen Field and T-Mobile Park. The quick-build changes tabbed for mid-2027 are intended to test a longer-term vision for a corridor that gets heavy usage on event days and is often trying to serve multiple different types of street users.
The Occidental Promenade is set to be the most visible product of Seattle's new People Streets and Public Spaces program, funded by the 2024 Seattle Transportation Levy .

Former Mayor Bruce Harrell directly inserted the promenade into his levy proposal, with support of stadium boosters including Seahawks chief operating officer David Young. The idea grew out of earlier efforts to improve Occidental Avenue, including a stadium district study that developed a streetscape plan in 2015, concepts that were ultimately put on a shelf to collect dust.

Final plans for the "near term" upgrades presented last week to Pioneer Square's Preservation District Board for approval show include chicanes, planters, street seating and micromobility corrals intended to carve out space along the wide street for pedestrian use. With the chicanes in place, the hope is for calmer traffic as drivers are prevented from picking up speed along a straight route of travel.

In a departure from most standard transportation projects, the Occidental Promenade is being managed by the Seattle Parks Foundation, in coordination with the Pioneer Square Alliance. The Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) will handle the design work. The Parks Foundation, a private non-profit organization that often bridges the gap between the City of Seattle and neighborhood groups interested in improving their park spaces, describes the promenade project as enabling a more "vibrant stadium district, providing street amenities and flexibility for the various users and venues."
The foundation also outlines a goal of better managing vending along the street. A future vending pilot program is expected to come back for separate approval at a later date.

"I would suggest it's probably the most hardworking street in downtown. We've got freight loading and unloading for the stadiums, which can range from, on a Taylor Swift concert, upwards of 20 to 25 semi trailers," said Jessa Timmer, Deputy Director at the Alliance for Pioneer Square, told the preservation board. "We've got pedestrian folks – during World Cup, we had, I don't even know how many, 150,000 to 200,000 pedestrians coming through Pioneer Square and this corridor. We've got back of house for many restaurants and businesses, sometimes front of house for those businesses."
"It's really a wide-ranging kind of ecosystem that's back here," Timmer said.

The improvements planned largely reinforce that ecosystem. The back-angle parking found across the street from Lumen Field will be retained, with a delineated walking path connecting the new nodes of pedestrian activity. Those paths will be most likely to be used on event days, creating a more orderly dispersal of pedestrian traffic when crowds are at their biggest.
It's less clear how utilized the planned seating will be on non-game days, with the street furniture essentially existing as an island in the middle of the street in some places.

"Our approach is really looking at a surface treatment and edge delineation to calm traffic and really work to improve that legibility and increase space for non-vehicular uses," SDOT project manager Ian Macek said.

The timeline to make the changes is currently dependent on Seattle City Light, which is planning work along Occidental in 2027, with promenade work to follow. But this phase will essentially act as a pilot to see how carving out pedestrian spaces works when it comes to the day-to-day operation of the street.

Though SDOT does need to receive a Certificate of Approval from the Pioneer Square Preservation Board to move forward with construction, that might not necessarily be the case with similar projects in the future. A legislative change put forward by Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck would explicitly exempt traffic control devices from requirements for buy-in from historic district boards like Pioneer Square's. Though the change has received a fair amount of pushback from historic preservation advocates , it is still heading for a council vote by early next year.

"These these improvements are inspired by the neighborhood context," Macek said. "They are temporary and reversible, and so this is really seen as a way to help pilot some of these options to see how they work, and also help inform that longer term before we commit to a design and advance that forward to be able to test things out, and really looking at materials that aren't impacting the historic resources along the corridor."
While billed as a "quick-build" intervention, the Occidental Promenade will still take more than two years from the launch of planning in early 2025 to implementation in mid-2027.

Other People Streets and Public Spaces projects are also moving forward at SDOT, including pedestrian plazas planned in Upper Queen Anne, Admiral, and Delridge. Unlike Occidental, those projects weren't specifically named in the 2024 levy but grew out of neighborhood support for creating pedestrian-forward spaces, building on past programs like the Pavement to Parks program abandoned under former Mayor Jenny Durkan.

Final approval to move forward with the Occidental Promenade is expected at a Pioneer Square Preservation District Board meeting before the end of the year. You can review the full plan set for Occidental Avenue here . The department also has active surveys up on SW Lander Street , 18th Avenue SW , and W Crocket Street .

articles.title: Taskforce Spells Out Need for Cabinet-Level Housing Agency in Washington
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: A final report approved Tuesday by a 19-member taskforce implores the state legislature to take action to stand up a new housing department in 2027, identifying gaps and inefficiencies that are standing in the way of the state's housing goals. The proposed department would be led by a cabinet-level Secretary of Housing and charged with "owning" outcomes around market-rate and affordable housing, including the production of more than one million new homes expected to be needed over the next two decades.

The taskforce was the product of an executive order issued by Governor Bob Ferguson last year, charged with creating a "clear mission and vision" for a new statewide housing department after the idea had been floating around for years. Currently, most housing-focused work is housed (so to speak) within the state's Commerce Department, with that workload increasing significantly over recent years as the legislature created new land use mandates and accountability frameworks.

The taskforce was chaired by former state Senator David Frockt, who currently serves as Ferguson's Deputy Policy Director for Healthcare, Housing, and Public Safety. Other heavy-hitters on the panel included State Senator Jessica Bateman, Pierce County Executive Ryan Mello, and Lieutenant Governor Denny Heck.

"Our task was challenging: build the framework for a new governing system for housing, while doing nothing to distract from the ongoing housing work that must continue even as we stand up a new agency," Frockt wrote in an introductory letter embedded in the report. "[Our report] gives policymakers recommendations they can consider in 2027: one accountable agency, built in phases, without disrupting the programs that people depend on today."
Frockt framed a state housing czar as the missing ingredient in a recipe that was otherwise coming together.

"Washington has the people and the programs to build the homes we need," Frockt continued. "What we have lacked is one cabinet-level official leading a single results-oriented agency that interacts with other state actors and local public and private partners in a spirit of innovation, acceleration, and red tape removal."
