Just last month, The Urbanist reported on new data showing that most housing growth targets around Central Puget Sound – an area that includes the state's largest growth centers – aren't being met, with overall rates of housing production since 2019 being carried by just a few jurisdictions, including Seattle. Of the 40 cities across King, Pierce, Snohomish and Kitsap Counties that are expected to accommodate the largest share of regional housing growth through 2044, just 14 are on track and many are significantly behind.

A spate of statewide housing reforms, including middle housing legalization, reduced parking requirements , and transit-oriented zoning mandates, have either gone into effect recently or set to be implemented in the coming years. Those reforms are expected to play a big role in moving the needle, but it will fall to the state to prod recalcitrant jurisdictions along.

One piece of that puzzle is the Housing Accountability Act , which reviews underperforming cities and towns on a rolling annual basis, provides guidance on how to get into compliance, and carries a major stick in the form of the "Builder's Remedy." Under that law, if a jurisdiction stays out-of-compliance with state law after being given an opportunity to make updates, they will have to approve any complete building permit as long as certain affordability thresholds are committed to, regardless of existing zoning.
So far, no Washington city has yet triggered it – although Bainbridge Island had flirted with testing the law.

"The recommendation responds to a housing system that produces too little housing despite substantial effort," the taskforce report's executive summary states. "To date, despite the more than 50 pieces of housing-related legislation that Washington has enacted in just the past five years, no state agency or the executive has established a single clear mission for a consolidated state housing department that encapsulates what the state is trying to do."

A phased implementation for the housing department would see a small startup team established alongside the housing secretary, using $5.38 million in seed funding in the next biennial budget. Four divisions would be established: data and performance, research and innovation, problem solving and partnerships, and standards and accountability. An initial strategic plan and an operating plan are both delivered during that phase, and a Washington Housing Results Council would be created and chaired by the secretary.

Phase two would occur during and after the 2028 legislative session, with programmatic functions and authorities officially moved into the new department and a "strategic housing action plan" established by that November. Phase three adds more programs and functions over time.

"With this phased approach, we're not waiting around for a new agency to build momentum and continue to advance the state's housing goals," said Amy Buckler, Assistant Director of Commerce's Housing Division. "We are concurrently working on the Washington Accelerator for Residential Production report, which is going to create a platform for building momentum and evolving. And we're doing that work concurrently with this."

Over the course of the taskforce's work, housing organizations of various stripes familiar with what it's like to navigate state government have weighed in on what could be achieved with a unified department, while clearly wanting to see more than a simple reorganization come out of the process.

"We believe the greatest benefit of this Department would be to serve as a visionary, central problem-solver and partner for affordable housing projects, the primary housing policy resource for the Legislature and Governor's Office, and a voice for the State in national housing policy discussions," Pamela Parr, President of the Washington Association of Housing Authorities, told the taskforce in letter this April. "In all these potential roles, the Department must be formed with an ingrained bias towards being a problem-solver in Washington State's housing framework, not a punitive enforcer of policy. This would be manifested in the vetting of projects (requiring skilled and knowledgeable staff), that once accepted, are supported by the Department in solving problems and removing barriers, even if those are from State policy."

With most of the big-ticket housing legislation checked off the legislature's to-do list, implementation and accountability will be a major focus over the coming years. The taskforce report clearly spells out a need for change, without proposing any bombshell changes that might make legislators skittish.

"I think that we have a practical, smart way forward that it can be recommended to Governor Ferguson to potentially propose to work with our colleagues in the legislature, both from a budgetary and policy standpoint," Frockt said ahead of a final vote to adopt the report. "We'll see how it all plays out in the current budget environment, but it's a smart, appropriate way forward that doesn't, I think, bite off too much initially, but also sets the stage for good work to come."

articles.title: Rinck seeks five council votes to block Capitol Hill and Central District camera rollout until SPD addresses risks
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: City Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck is calling for support for her budget proviso that would pause the expansion of Seattle’s Real Time Crime Center police cameras until recommendations from the Office of the Inspector General are satisfied.

The move follows Mayor Katie Wilson’s decision to lift her pause on the expansion as Seattle Police officials say they are working to respond to a privacy audit of the system identified constitutional risks, technological shortfalls, and policy gaps. Recent reviews under the Office of Inspector General made similar findings .

Saying she has “deep concerns about surveillance technology from civil rights implications, policy oversight gaps, and the efficacy of this technology,” Rinck said Wednesday that the proviso is supported by South Seattle Councilmember Eddie Lin and Rinck’s fellow citywide representative Dionne Foster but requires five votes to pass.
“Final votes in budget start on Friday. Now is the time to make your voice heard,” Rinck posted in her social media statement on the proposal.

The Office of Inspector General recommended that the Seattle Police Department implement case numbers and formal justifications within the Axon Fusus software before analysts can view camera feeds to prevent unauthorized or proactive surveillance. It also urged the department and city leaders to establish clear policies and privacy safeguards for integrating privately owned security cameras, including geographic boundaries, protocols to avoid monitoring non-public spaces, and retention limits, while enforcing stricter search logging and civil liberty controls across stored surveillance databases like Automated License Plate Readers.

The Seattle City Council is wrapping up the city’s long budget season with final adjustments to the mayor’s 2027-2028 budget plan including tapping $31 million in JumpStart payroll tax reserves and cutting $22 million in pension transfers to reverse cuts proposed by the mayor to address a looming budget deficit.

CHS reported in March as Wilson followed up on campaign promises and stopped an expansion of the city’s police camera system to the stadium district, Capitol Hill’s nightlife areas, and 23rd Ave in the Central District citing concerns about how law enforcement and federal authorities might access the technology and data.
The cameras for Capitol Hill — budgeted but never installed — would cover Broadway from Capitol Hill Station to Pike/Pine and the core of the Pike/Pine nightlife zone.

In the Central District, the camera system will be centered around safety at Garfield High School with boundaries running from a block north of the school along E Cherry all the way to S Jackson. The western edge has been planned to include 20th Ave and the eastern edge would extend along 26th Ave.

The Capitol Hill system is estimated to cost around $400,000 to install and $35,000 a year to operate. The Central District installation has a budget of $425,000 and also an estimated $35,000 in “ongoing annual costs.”

articles.title: 1,000+ reports a year — Sweeps in Cal Anderson Park are rare but neighborhood encampment complaints tell a different story
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Tents along the east edge of the park included in an October clearance report — one of three clearances logged in 2026

Facing escalating neighborhood friction around Capitol Hill’s central park, the Greater Seattle Business Association has pushed back against City Hall , calling for a halt to homeless encampment removals in Cal Anderson .

The pushback comes as Mayor Katie Wilson says she is shifting the city’s encampment strategy to prioritize clearance of public spaces like sidewalks and parks while pairing the efforts with increased services and shelter.

In a statement addressed to the mayor, the LGBTQ+ and allied business advocacy group that bills itself as Capitol HIll’s chamber of commerce challenged the assertion that restaurant, shop, and property owners have asked for stepped-up enforcement.

“We request that Mayor Wilson immediately order a pause on all sweeps of Cal Anderson Park until this issue is meaningfully resolved,” the letter states, signed by GSBA Capitol Hill Neighborhood Safety Manager Jen Carl and Policy and Advocacy Director Gabriel Neuman .
The leadership pushed back directly against city outreach teams:

It has also come to our attention that the Unified Care Team has been referencing the business community to justify harmful encampment removals that do not adhere to the policies and laws set forth by the city. This statement is both inappropriate and inaccurate. While some individuals may support these initiatives, our overall Capitol Hill community, including the vast majority of our business owners, firmly oppose such punitive and unnecessary measures.

The GSBA expressed alarm over “harassment and intimidation of our unhoused trans and LGBTQ+ siblings” by the Unified Care Team and Seattle Police Department officers, urging an independent review alongside expanded harm-reduction investments like handwashing stations, sharps containers, and funding for mutual aid and community groups including Stone Soup Crew, MANTIS, and the Cal Anderson Park Alliance.
Earlier this year , CHS reported on CAPA calling on the city to increase maintenance and outreach resources at the park citing public safety concerns.
GSBA’s new demand for an immediate pause in sweeps comes as city records shows relatively rare full clearance activity in the park.
According to “Site Journal” records published by the Seattle Human Services Department , the city has logged only three formal encampment clearances for Cal Anderson in all of 2026:

By comparison, the city logged two site journals for the park in 2025 (August and December) and only one in 2023, with none archived under Cal Anderson in the portal between 2017 and 2022 or throughout 2024.

While daily field contacts, bag-and-tag garbage runs, and park ranger moves can occur without triggering a formal HSD site journal, full-scale removal operations in Cal Anderson have officially averaged just one every few months.
Though clearance logs show infrequent full sweeps, citizen reports from the ground tell a different story.
Data from the city’s Find It Fix It customer service portal tracking reported unauthorized encampments reveals an aggressive rebound in complaints surrounding the park in 2026:
The records show where community tension concentrates. Rather than spreading across the park’s interior lawns, reports are pinned to perimeter sidewalks and transit borders:
Meanwhile, Seattle City Hall is setting the spending plan for 2027 including how the city will step up its own efforts as the King County Regional Homelessness Authority is ramped down .

A key debate focuses on the the Unified Care Team and Wilson’s plan which preserves core funding for rapid encampment and obstruction removals versus City Council efforts to impose stricter oversight and push resources toward harm reduction. Facing a significant deficit balanced in part by tapping JumpStart payroll expense tax reserves, council members and community stakeholders are pushing budget provisos that would condition the team’s funding on reporting regarding shelter referral outcomes, property storage compliance, and law enforcement costs.
Council proposals could open spending on new handwashing stations and public toilets and closer operational alignment with the CARE department’s unarmed alternative crisis response teams.

The Wilson administration is slowing its homelessness and shelter goals as part of spending shifts to address a projected $175 million budget deficit. While Wilson’s core goals remain in place including the establishment of approximately 1,000 emergency shelter spaces paired with wraparound services, budget realities will mean a slower approach.
Wilson also vetoed a plan to create a RV parking permit system tied to shelter and services, saying it would not be a cost-effective program.

Earlier this year, the administration framed the delivery of 1,000 shelter units as a single-year objective for 2026. The administration has now extended that goal through the end of 2027, scheduling 960 total beds to serve an estimated 1,750 people annually across facilities established in 2026 and eight sites slated for 2027.

According to a 2026 count across King County , the number of unsheltered individuals jumped from around 9,800 in 2024 to 11,829 in 2026, a 21% increase in people living on the streets, in vehicles, or in parks.
In the meantime, neighbors and passersby are logging nearly three encampment reports a day this year in Cal Anderson Park.

articles.title: Syd’s Moore Theatre Show Was Gay Church
articles.author: Julianne Bell
paras: Alternative R&B singer and producer Syd named her third full-length solo album Beard as a nod to growing out her “peach fuzz” mustache. The title couldn’t be more appropriate as she embraces her own standards of attractiveness and steps into a more secure, mature era as a newly sober, married queer woman, and she brought that newfound confidence to her performance at the Moore Theatre last night.

The second night of the Beard tour opened with a set from rising South Seattle R&B artist Jaymin, who had a voice like molten honey. Then Syd herself bounded onto stage in a floppy red beanie. She worked the crowd expertly, pointing to fans, dancing with the mic stand all over the stage, and making everyone in the room feel like she was singing just to them. During the track “No Looking Back,” she handed the mic to a woman in the front row, who belted into it with impressive pitch. “Then that Jasmin 17, rub up on your body / Sensual and enticin’, you know just how I like it,” Syd sang over the lush grooves of “Jasmin 17,” an ode to her lover’s Le Labo fragrance. As I jotted notes in my writing pad, I felt like Hannah Einbinder in Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma , when she dramatically scribbles “DESIRE” in her notebook and underlines it multiple times. It struck me that I’ve rarely witnessed any queer female artist, much less a Black masc one, express desire as openly and matter-of-factly as Syd—the closest I’ve seen would be Chappell Roan, who is white and has a high-femme stage persona, or MUNA, which has two white members and a femme frontwoman. It was a radical, near-spiritual experience to watch so many people of all orientations and genders responding to her raw emotion in real time. The audience swayed on their feet with hands raised, and it gave the illusion of a church congregation.

“Tonight I’m gonna swim in it, dive in it, drown in it, hide in it, babe,” she promised with all the unbridled yearning of Boyz II Men during the one-minute-and-10-second-long “Drown In It” (which is about exactly what you think it is). Some fangirls dissolved into giggles and shrieks at the suggestive lyrics, filling the room with the giddy energy of a boy band concert or school dance. The song segued into “Body,” which is arguably her sultriest song and had couples wrapped around each other and making out. Let’s just say that if strap could impregnate, there’d be a lot of babies conceived after this show. Syd guided first the “ladies,” then the “fellas,” in the audience through a call-and-response for the “yeah yeah yeah yeah” choruses and jokingly ordered one man to stand up.

She led the crowd in hand claps for “Fast Car,” which is not, as the title suggests, a cover of the tragic Tracy Chapman classic, but rather a carefree, sexy number about being, ahem, knee-deep in the passenger seat—“I wanted to make something for the gay Black girls. I want them to see themselves in this and in me,” Syd said in a statement when the song was released in 2021. In the video, she and her now-wife, model Ariana Simone, drive through the desert in their Bronco and stop for some covert vehicular activity. “Take me there, I wanna ride,” she crooned, and fans joyfully sang along with every word.

Despite her self-assurance and showmanship, Syd also wasn’t afraid to show glimpses into her vulnerable side. “I really needed this today,” she confessed, explaining that she’d been sad all day. “You can’t help but wonder sometimes how much longer you’ll be able to do the thing you love.”

At another point, she explained that she started her career as a studio engineer: “It’s not the flex you think it is. I had to learn how to sing on the go.” “You did a good job!” boomed someone in response, and she laughed and thanked them. “You never know where life will take you. I attribute my success to taking the opportunities that were in front of me, whether I’m ready or not,” she said, “and I would encourage you all to do the same.”

“We love you, Syd!” a devotee screamed. “It’s nice to know you’re loved,” Syd reflected. “It’s nice when people say it out loud, in public.” Then she seamlessly launched into the song “Out Loud,” which bares her insecurities in a new relationship: “I can’t ignore it / Don’t understand / Why you haven’t told your friends / I wish you would call them / Tell them everything about me.”

Later in the set, Syd played a series of several songs by other artists for which she’s become well-known, including “YOU’RE THE ONE” by Kaytranada (on which she is featured) and “Girl” by the Internet, the alt R&B/soul band she formed with fellow Odd Future member Matt Martians in early 2011. “Shout-out to great collaborators,” she said. Toward the end of the show, she thanked her fans for their support and said “none of this would be possible” without them.
“Thank you guys for sticking around for the dream,” she said. “Who knows what I’ll be next?”
The post Syd’s Moore Theatre Show Was Gay Church appeared first on The Stranger .

articles.title: A Newborn Died in a Faith-Healing Sect. The State — and One Ex-Believer — Stepped in to Save Her Twin.
articles.author: Noelle Crombie
paras: The deputy medical examiner thought the family was being evasive. Eric Tonsfeldt had been dispatched to the pistachio-green house in Oregon City on the night of March 5, 2017. Inside he found Sarah Mitchell in bed, her dead newborn in her arms.

Mitchell is a member of the Followers of Christ, a sect known for refusing medical treatment. She had received no prenatal care. Three women without medical training guided her delivery that afternoon.

Tonsfeldt listened as the family insisted that the baby, whom they had named Ginnifer, had seemed healthy for most of the afternoon, then suddenly stopped breathing. They couldn’t explain why the baby appeared so underweight. Their answers to many of Tonsfeldt’s questions were vague. Nobody would make eye contact with him.

Later, investigators would discover that 13 minutes after Ginnifer’s birth, Followers began exchanging a series of worried texts. “Not good breathing,” one wrote in a group chat. Another requested prayers: “She’s really bad.” (One person in the chat would later advise deleting the messages.)

No one had called 911 as the gaps between each breath increased. When asked why not, Ginnifer’s father later said, “Because it’s in God’s hands.” He anointed his daughter with olive oil and wept as he prayed that she would be OK. Ginnifer died in his arms at 7 p.m., four hours after she was born.
Tonsfeldt gently collected the newborn and examined her in another room. She weighed 3½ pounds, roughly half that of an average full-term infant. He found no signs of injury or trauma.

The medical examiner still felt that something was awry. To play for time, he asked if someone would make him a cup of coffee and headed to the kitchen. As Tonsfeldt waited, one of the baby’s grandfathers approached him and blurted out an unexpected question: Would it make a difference if Ginnifer had a twin?
There was another baby, a girl named Evelyn. She was alive.
In the dim light of a bathroom, Tonsfeldt found women huddled over a tiny newborn, who was barely making a sound. They were feeding her from an eyedropper.

He told the family to get her to a hospital. After Evelyn’s grandfather made it clear they weren’t going anywhere, Tonsfeldt summoned the police, who delivered an ultimatum: Take Evelyn to the hospital or they’d do it themselves.

Evelyn’s family relented. A patrol car followed to make sure they got there. She was admitted to a neonatal intensive care unit in Portland with respiratory distress syndrome. With the help of a breathing machine and a feeding tube, Evelyn began to stabilize. An autopsy would later conclude the same condition, common in premature babies, had caused her sister’s death.
The Mitchells were charged with murder by neglect, as well as criminal mistreatment for failing to get Evelyn medical care. That left authorities with another challenge: Who would care for Evelyn?

Her family assumed any custody arrangement would be temporary and suggested Marshall and Jennifer Phillips, a couple born and raised in the Followers. But Marshall was no ordinary Follower. Once, when his young son became gravely ill, he brought him to a hospital. In the eyes of the state, that made Marshall and his wife suitable candidates to look after Evelyn.

Evelyn’s family didn’t know then that Marshall’s choice to save his son had set him on a yearslong journey, one that would eventually lead him away from the only life he’d ever known. And that he would take Evelyn with him.

For more than a century, states have wrestled with how to address the deaths of children whose parents refuse them medical care for religious reasons. As early as 1901, a father in New York who believed in the “power of God to heal the sick through prayer” was prosecuted for failing to call a doctor for his young daughter who died from pneumonia. Since then, courts have repeatedly held — in cases where Christian Scientists refused treatment or Jehovah’s Witnesses declined blood transfusions — that adults are free to reject medical care for themselves.
Whether they can be compelled to provide medical care for their children is another matter, one that’s been left to states to decide. Courts have generally deferred to legislatures on this question.

Marshall Phillips was raised in the Followers of Christ, which forbids medical care. When his son fell gravely ill, he took him to the hospital. That choice set him on a yearslong journey, one that would eventually lead him away from the only life he’d ever known.

For decades, Oregon’s law gave latitude to faith healing and authorities did little to intervene. Between 1989 and 1999, 18 children of the Oregon City-based Followers died. (The sect numbered between 1,500 and 2,000 at its peak.) Most or all of those deaths were preventable, according to the state medical examiner at the time, who estimated that the child death rate in the sect was 26 times that of the general population.

The revelation of those deaths, in The Oregonian and other news outlets, prompted state lawmakers to act. In 1999, they removed spiritual treatment as a defense for second-degree manslaughter and criminal mistreatment. In 2008, prosecutors filed their first case against Followers parents after a 15-month-old died from untreated bronchial pneumonia and a blood infection. A jury convicted the girl’s father of a single count of criminal mistreatment, a misdemeanor, and acquitted her mother.

Two more children in the sect died without medical attention during this period, prompting the Legislature in 2011 to do away with the spiritual defense for any crime. Among those supporting the change: the Christian Science church, which by then had softened its stance amid a steep decline in membership. In a letter to lawmakers that year, a church official wrote: “Spiritual care should never be practiced at the expense of a child’s life.”

Changes in Oregon law — and prosecutors’ willingness to pursue parents who watched their children die — spurred a slow but perceptible shift: Deaths of children in the Followers have become an anomaly. Ginnifer Mitchell’s death in 2017 came amid that yearslong decline. Since then, one child has died due to lack of medical care.

During this same time frame in Idaho, where the laws protect parents who rely only on faith healing, reporting by ProPublica found at least 11 babies and children of Followers died from treatable conditions.

Still, Ginnifer’s death shows how the most entrenched elements of faith-healing communities resist aggressive enforcement. Sarah Mitchell chose to give birth without doctors or nurses, even as her sister was in prison for failing to provide medical care for her premature newborn, who died in 2009. And Sarah’s lack of prenatal care was such that she realized she was carrying twins only when her labor continued after her first baby emerged.
Evelyn might not have survived if police didn’t have the law on their side, allowing them to intervene and demand that her parents take her to the hospital.

The stories of Evelyn and Marshall Phillips — still the subject of legal proceedings today — offer a rare view into the closed community and reveal both the power and the limits of the state’s efforts to compel parents to seek medical care for their children.

Marshall’s ancestors were among the earliest members of the Followers, whose history dates to the late 1800s, when faith-healing sects were active in the Midwest. The faithful later migrated west, starting congregations in Idaho. In the 1930s, a charismatic Followers preacher named Walter White left Idaho for Oregon City, then a lively hub for the timber and paper industries. White’s emotional sermons earned him the moniker “the crying preacher.”

Followers believed the devout earned their place in the afterlife through good acts. They also believed that God heals. The doctrine stems from a passage in the Book of James, which proclaims “And the prayer of faith shall save the sick, and the Lord shall raise him up.” Seeking medical care was viewed as an abandonment of faith. Those who visited doctors risked being shunned.
By the 1950s, White broke ties with other Followers congregations. He later said that Christ had visited him in a dream and told him the world would soon end and so would baptisms.

White died in 1969 at age 67. Baptisms ended after that, effectively sealing the faithful from the outside world. The Followers never identified White’s successor. To this day, the congregation has no pastor. The lack of a spiritual leader seems only to have intensified members’ influence on one another.
The sect’s practices include other unusual elements: The Bible doesn’t figure in their services, which consist mostly of congregants singing hymns.

In many respects, Followers lead conventional lives. As a boy born in 1975, Marshall rode his bike, ate sugary treats, watched TV and listened to 1980s rock bands like Van Halen. His parents took him and his siblings camping and saved up for trips to Disneyland.

But his life was also circumscribed by his faith. Several times a week, he accompanied his parents to functions at the beige meetinghouse set back from busy Molalla Avenue in Oregon City. Starting at age 7, Followers’ children are separated by gender and age into their own pews. Marshall understood that he would grow up, and grow old, with the kids seated around him. He was instructed not to befriend kids outside the church. Followers considered them “worldly,” the sect’s derisive term for those focused on terrestrial, rather than celestial, concerns.

Like his peers, Marshall never visited a pediatrician. He was never vaccinated. His mom anointed his forehead with extra virgin olive oil when his head throbbed. He endured chicken pox and whooping cough and eventually recovered from both — proof, he believed, of God’s healing powers.
His parents, like others in the sect, made exceptions for dental care. They accepted the use of Novocain but refused the ibuprofen the dentist recommended to address lingering pain after a procedure.

Marshall knew from a young age that his future would be determined by the church. He figured he’d work for a Follower. He’d marry one, too. Marshall and Jennifer went on their first date in a courtship ritual the Followers call a carload — small groups of teens who drive together to get ice cream or coffee. She was 14 and he was 18. They married when Jennifer turned 17, the age girls in the Followers typically wed.

Jennifer’s father had died the year before, surrounded by men from the church. Members were expected to care for the dying, with men tending to men and women to women. Her father never went to the doctor, and family members think he died from heart failure. He was 37.

Women typically give birth in their parents’ homes, and Jennifer was no exception. She delivered her first child, Mary, in the living room, attended by her mother, her mother-in-law, aunts and other women. Marshall was there, too. The rest of the men waited out of sight, smoke from their cigarettes drifting into the living room. She had two more children after that, both sons.

Today, at 50, Marshall looks like the epitome of a suburban dad. With his receding hairline, beard and broad physique, you could picture him browsing the aisles of The Home Depot. He possesses a gentle quality and doesn’t shy away from even harsh self-reflection.

The Followers abide by what they view as traditional gender roles, with men leading their households. Many male Followers work as contractors, electricians and plumbers; Marshall works as a consultant for a heating and air conditioning company. Women mostly focus on the home and their children. Jennifer cleans houses to supplement their income and homeschooled their kids for a time.

As a Follower, Marshall said he pressured his children to fit in at church. He believed the sect’s teachings about earning one’s way to salvation, and he spent many Sunday afternoons visiting the sick and caring for the dying. He and his wife never challenged the institution that shaped their lives.

articles.title: Prophecy, Scorn and a Rejection of This World: The Forbidding Vision of a Faith-Healing Preacher
articles.author: Noelle Crombie
paras: It was a stark and forbidding vision for those who followed the righteous path. Scorn, the preacher told his congregation, was a person’s lot if they led an “honest, clean, pure, godly life.” The world hated “people that live like that,” he said.
“They want you to be just as ungodly and filthy as they are,” he said in a rare audio recording, obtained by The Oregonian/OregonLive, of a 1958 sermon.

The preacher was Walter White, who led an Oregon City offshoot of the Followers of Christ, an Idaho sect that spurns medical treatment as a show of faith. White was a grocer, originally from Picabo, Idaho, whose congregants came to view as a prophet. He rambled at times during his sermon but always returned to simple and severe messages about choosing righteousness rather than the ways of the world. A trim figure in wire-rim glasses and dark combed-back hair, he spoke in a voice that evoked the stentorian tones of an old newsreel announcer. In the scratchy recording, people cough and babies cry as he preaches.

White was uneasy about being taped, according to a note by the congregant who made the recording. White didn’t want his message to fall into what he thought were undesirable hands. He viewed disbelievers with disgust. They put their trust in human experts, such as doctors, rather than in God. People like that, he told the faithful, “want to be somebody.” They want “the wisdom of the world and admiration.”

Today, nearly 60 years after White’s death, his pronouncements continue to influence the faithful. For many Followers, White remained “the highest authority,” said Mark Shaw, who left the sect in 2019 and keeps in touch with some Followers. Members invoked his teachings to settle disagreements. “It was used as the trump card,” he said. “It was the discussion-ender.”
To understand the modern-day Oregon City congregation, it’s essential to examine White’s role. No pastor ever succeeded him, leaving the sect all the more reliant on his teachings.

The Oregonian/OregonLive and ProPublica have published a series of articles in recent months about the Followers of Christ in Oregon and Idaho , focusing on the long history of parents in Followers congregations declining to seek medical care for their critically ill children and the sometimes fatal consequences .

Little has been publicly known about White, likely due to the Followers’ culture of isolation and secrecy. The Oregonian/OregonLive was able to piece together details through documents we obtained, including biographical sketches, a transcript and the recording of the sermon, along with written accounts of dreams White purported to have and records of baptisms he performed. Among the documents was a list of his prophecies and even a sex guide he disseminated.

White was born into the Followers, whose members migrated to Idaho from the Midwest around the turn of the 20th century. Men in White’s family preached, and he joined them in his 20s, the story goes, after he dreamed that worms would devour him if he didn’t.

In the early 1930s, White joined two church elders on a journey from Idaho to Oregon City to minister to a dying man. After talking with them, the man readily discarded his medications and was relieved to see White, an avid smoker, roll a cigarette because the man didn’t want to kick the habit. For the next five years, White traveled between Idaho and Oregon to preach and by 1938, he had moved to Oregon to lead a fledgling congregation.

Followers at the time were led by a constellation of preachers and elders, all men. Notes from one of their meetings in 1937 revealed that Followers believed White possessed the “gift of prophecy.” It also recorded the debates that simmered among them — whether women should be allowed to cut their hair, for instance. They talked about the value of dictionaries, which some classified as “worldly” items to be avoided, and determined that women assisting with home births should not “look under the cover” as women labored. One account written years later by a Follower suggested that White split with a prominent Idaho preacher after revelations that the man had sexual contact with a 15-year-old girl.

Some of those values still shape the Followers today. Congregants tend to stay out of what they view as the worldly affairs of politics and civic life, and they generally don’t pursue education beyond high school or vocational training. The Followers remain patriarchal; men are expected to lead their households.

White was known among Followers as “brother Walter.” An undated black-and-white photograph shows him baptizing a child in what appears to be a baptismal pool, his arm raised in prayer. In another image dated 1951, he wears a suit jacket and tie, a mug in one hand and a cigarette in the other.

As much a ruler as a spiritual leader, White enjoyed near-absolute authority. Followers believed he possessed such divine power that he knew their thoughts and secrets. They turned to him for approval on matters both consequential and mundane, from marital advice to appliance purchases. (White even weighed in on where to shop: He owned a local market and made it clear he expected to see Followers there.)

White’s earthly teachings extended to a perhaps unexpected realm: Couples on the cusp of marriage received a sex guide, which continued to be distributed as recently as 2018. Complete with explicit detail and anatomical diagrams, the 15-page manual includes chapters titled “the ideal love act” and “the control of climax.” And, in a seeming exception to the prohibition on medical treatment, it goes so far as to recommend that women who feel inhibited should consider seeing a doctor “who has given the sex problems sincere study.”

White preached the Oregon City sect’s singularity: His flock was spiritually superior to other Follower congregations, he contended, including ones in Idaho and Grants Pass, Oregon. By the 1950s, he had cut off ties to those groups.

In 1965, White told his congregation of his prophecy that the end times were near. He recounted a dream, which he said was set against the backdrop of the Kennedy Space Center in Florida, that involved walking with Jesus Christ, according to one account. He dreamed they climbed a launchpad, and White noted he was impressed with Christ’s physical agility. Days before White shared his vision, NASA launched Gemini 3, the first U.S. mission to send multiple astronauts into space.

White told the faithful that it was during this dream that Christ said the world would come to an end in six years. He said Christ warned that baptisms among the Followers would end even sooner. That his apocalyptic prophecy fizzled didn’t shake Followers’ faith.

White died in 1969. He was seen as irreplaceable. A handful of elders divided his leadership duties but lacked White’s authority. The faithful never tapped a successor, believing only a man called by God could fill the role. No one was ever deemed worthy enough to take his place.

But one element of White’s prophecy did come true. Given that he was the only person who could perform baptisms, his passing also meant that the ritual ended. As a result, the flock, which former members say numbered 1,500 or more at its peak, today consists solely of generations of the same families who were members in 1969.

Like other elders in the early days of the Followers, White saw illness as a test of faith. During the 1937 meeting, about 18 elders and preachers from congregations in Idaho and Oregon gathered at the Oregon City meetinghouse to settle the rules that would shape the church, according to a written account compiled by sect members years later.

The men discussed the Book of James in the New Testament, which says, “And the prayer of faith shall save the sick, and the Lord shall raise him up.” Followers interpret the lines as an edict to rely only on faith when faced with illness. The passage would be “strictly enforced to show faith,” according to an account of the meeting compiled years later. They believed that death, if it came, was God’s will.

Years later, in 1965, when the state investigated the case of a teen in the sect whose broken ankle had gone untreated, White said, “faith can heal,” according to a story in The Oregonian at the time. “We believe that God comes before man. If a person’s faith doesn’t go far enough, then he can seek help from man.”

The consequences of this belief system still reverberate. For years, the Oregon City Followers suffered multiple child deaths, many from treatable or preventable conditions. The deaths prompted the Legislature in 1999 to chip away at legal protections for parents whose children died without medical care. Then in 2011, lawmakers removed all protections for faith healing.

The faith-healing doctrine would affect White’s own descendants. Two of his great-granddaughters spent years in prison for failing to seek medical care for their premature newborns who died. In 2017, one of his great-great-granddaughters, Evelyn, suffered respiratory complications related to her premature birth. Authorities attribute her survival to the intervention of law enforcement officials who ordered her parents to get her to the hospital. Evelyn’s life and journey out of the Followers is the subject of a story and documentary published by The Oregonian/OregonLive and ProPublica.
The post Prophecy, Scorn and a Rejection of This World: The Forbidding Vision of a Faith-Healing Preacher appeared first on ProPublica .

articles.title: King County Metro planning service changes for new Renton Transit Center
articles.author: Alex Kvenvolden
paras: As part of the Stride S1 line, Sound Transit is building a new transit center in Renton, adjacent to the existing South Renton Park and Ride. When it opens in 2028, it will be known as simply Renton Transit Center, and will replace both the existing Renton Transit Center in downtown Renton, and the adjacent South Renton Park and Ride. Commuters need not fret over lack of parking, as the new transit center will include a new garage dedicated for commuter parking that is larger than the parking at both current facilities that are reserved for transit commuters. With the transit center moving, bus service has to move with it, and Metro has made its first service proposal on what that may look like in its Renton Area Mobility Project (RAMP). Details below the jump.

King County Metro is proposing moving every route that serves the current Renton Transit Center in downtown Renton to the future Renton Transit Center. Multiple services (including both RapidRide lines) will continue to downtown Renton, but the relocated transit center will be the new transfer hub for all routes.

To move the connection point, routes 148 and 153 (which already serve the South Renton P&R before continuing to the current transit center) are going to be shortened to the new transit center (and not continue downtown). Routes 105, 240, and 907 are going to be lengthened further south to reach the new transit center. Routes 106 and 107 are going to be redirected away from downtown to the new transit center, and routes 101, 102, RapidRides F and I (current 160) lines are seeing no substantial change in routing.

Additionally, route 153 will move to operate on SW 7th St to Lind Ave in both directions, and the RapidRide F Line will move off of SW 7th, Lind Ave, and SW 16th St to run on SW Grady Way from the new Renton Transit Center to Oaksdale Ave SW. Lastly, the two Metro Flex zones serving the existing transit center will be adjusted to both cover the relocated transit center.

Service levels across most routes are going to be the same, but there are some exceptions. The most welcome change in my opinion is that route 907 will be expanded to start earlier and run later (6am to 6pm). Currently, the 907 doesn’t serve peak direction commutes at all, because historically these were covered by route 143 (e.g., northbound trips in the morning peak were all 143 trips, and after the commute is done, route 907 would start running). As a result, the last trip of the “night” on route 907 to Black Diamond from Renton TC leaves at 3:45pm (because route 143 would start covering that trip shortly after that). However, route 143 is still suspended, as it has been since 2020. Metro’s proposal will finally delete route 143 about 8 years after it was suspended, with the freed up service hours being used to expand service on route 907 and to implement the rest of the plan.

One other change in service is that short route 102 trips (which are ones that go from Seattle to S. Renton P&R, but not to Fairwood) will be converted to route 101. The same number of trips will run from Seattle to both Renton and Fairwood, but service will be simplified so that all 102 trips go to Renton TC and Fairwood, and all 101 trips will go to Renton TC and downtown Renton.

While the plan does a decent job at connecting current service to the Stride station at the new transit center, it does not provide any connections to the other Stride station in Renton at NE 44th St. I think this is a particularly unfortunate omission because parking at this station was delayed to the mid 2030s in the first realignment plan, meaning that for its first several years, the NE 44th St Station will only be useful for people going to or from walking distance of the station itself. A bus route connecting the station to the frequent route 240 a couple miles east could give local residents a way to access nearby Stride service, but as it stands, Stride service at NE 44th will be completely unusable for many local residents until the parking garage is completed.
I asked King County Metro if they had considered adding connections to NE 44th St, including a concept route that is part of their Metro Connects interim map, and I got this response:

The implementation of a new route to serve this station was not part of the scope of the Renton Area Mobility Project. As a budget-constrained project, the focus is on trying to facilitate the transit center relocation (which would require more operating resources than on the ground today, as more routes need to be extended to the new facility than there are routes that can be truncated at the new facility), without a reduction to current service levels. That task alone was challenging, and there unfortunately isn’t remaining project budget to pursue service growth at the scale of implementing a new route like [the route from Metro Connects].

While it is probably the correct decision to keep this particular project narrowly focused on the area around downtown Renton due to how many routes need to be changed in this one area and the limited amount of service hours to work with, I do hope Metro is able to secure more funding for the other station in the near future, and will evaluate potential service options whether or not they can budget additional service hours.

When I first got familiar with route 101, it was different than today. Rather than starting at South Renton P&R, then going to Renton TC, then Seattle, it actually did the Renton area “backwards”, by starting at Renton TC, then going south a bit to South Renton P&R, then going to Seattle. I always thought this was odd, because Renton TC was clearly the dominant transit hub, and also because it was going to the south park and ride before heading back north.

With south Renton being the transit hub starting in 2028, I think it makes sense to bring back the “backwards” route 101. It will save transferring riders about 10 minutes on each trip, which is quite significant!
If you have any thoughts on the proposal, sound off below, and be sure to take Metro’s survey by November 30.

articles.title: WSDOT Seeks Feedback in I-5 High Speed Rail Survey
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: State officials are trying to keep the dream alive of high speed rail connecting the Cascadia region and linking Seattle, Portland, and Vancouver. The Washington State Department of Transportation (WSDOT) has a public survey open through November 13.

The survey will refine high speed rail options while also shaping the I-5 master plan the agency is putting together at the same time. Yoking together the planning for the region's primary freeway and its most promising HSR route was a conscious decision on WSDOT's part, aiming to underscore the crash course the region is on toward transportation gridlock – at least without significant intervention.

"The Cascadia megaregion is expected to grow by 3.4 million more people by 2050. This growth is equivalent to adding a city almost the size of Los Angeles to the megaregion," WSDOT noted on its project page . "The increase in population will be matched by economic growth across industries like technology, aerospace, healthcare and logistics. Recent studies show that the strain on our existing transportation system will be significant by 2050."

The survey does not provide much new information for folks who have already been engaged in this high speed rail process, which WSDOT has long been exploring – going back to a 2017 feasibility study , a 2019 business case study , and a 2020 framework study outlining a path to cross-border governmental collaboration.
WSDOT did share a project definition that sets a goal of achieving top speeds of at least 160 miles per hour.

"The purpose of the Cascadia High-Speed Rail project is to provide reliable high-speed rail service at speeds greater than 160 mph or 260 kph that is competitive with other transportation modes and improves mobility between the Cascadia megaregion’s metropolitan areas. The project purpose includes optimizing the safe and efficient movement of people in the growing Cascadia megaregion and facilitating economic development."

According to a presentation from September at the Washington Transportation Commission, the high speed rail program is spending the next year identifying "potentially feasible" route options, before spending another year refining those options.

"The Service Development Plan will be an analysis of potential routes where high speed rail could operate, an analysis of conceptual service options like the number of train trips and the number of stops that a high speed service may have," Ben Tripousis, WSDOT's Cascadia High-Speed Rail and I-5 Program Administrator told the commission. "We'll look at financing and governance as a component of the service development plan development. What the service development plan will not determine is a preferred route option or specific station locations at this time. That will be accomplished in future analysis."

WSDOT clarified that HSR would be a complement rather than a replacement for existing Amtrak Cascades service: "Cascadia High-Speed Rail would complement the existing Amtrak Cascades passenger rail service. High-speed rail would make fewer stops and travel at greater speeds than conventional rail services, likely running on new, dedicated tracks. Think of high-speed rail as the express train, while Amtrak Cascades would be the local route."

WSDOT is leading on the planning effort because 277 of the 315 miles between Portland and Vancouver, B.C. are in Washington state. That stretch could be spanned in as little as two hours with high speed rail, depending on the number of stops and the maximum speeds achieved.
In the final days of the Biden Administration, WSDOT secured a $49.7 million federal grant to fund the creation a service development plan for Cascadia high-speed rail.

WSDOT will likely be facing pressure from some quarters to widen I-5 in its master plan process. Former WSDOT secretary Roger Millar warned that widening I-5 would be prohibitively expansive and ineffective, since car traffic would swell to clog the wider artery.

High speed rail would be pricey in its own right, but with much better ability to scale up and solve the underlying problem. Unlike adding another freeway lane on I-5, high-speed rail can boost frequency to meet increased demand, rather than quickly succumbing to congestion issues and getting trapped in a cycle of induced demand .

Whether freeway expansions or light rail , large infrastructure projects are facing massive increases in construction costs, which is sure to impact high-speed rail projects as well. These cost increases are tied to a period of high inflation and sky-high costs on construction materials (linked to Trump tariffs) and fuel (tied to Trump's war in Iran). In its 2017 study, WSDOT estimated Cascadia “ultra-high speed rail” would cost between $24 billion and $42 billion — and that was before the era of high construction cost escalation hit.
A higher price tag is running headlong into a period of retreating public investment in passenger rail.

Republicans have also been pushing to overhaul grant programs funded in Biden's Infrastructure and Jobs Act to punish transit projects. Now that Democrats have retaken control of Congress, gutting transit investment seemingly should be off the agenda – although some Democrats like Washington's own Rep. Rick Larsen (who is the frontrunner to secure the coveted position of House transportation committee chair) had signed on the Republican-led legislation, which has an Orwellian name: the BUILD America 250 Act.

Meanwhile, some rail advocates have argued high speed rail has boondoggle potential – pointing to the over budget and very behind schedule California high speed rail project – as they push the state should prioritize more incremental improvements to Amtrak Cascades service that could be achieved sooner. Studies have shown high demand for conventional rail that could easily support doubling Cascades frequencies to 16 daily trips – which state lawmakers affirmed as a goal without yet allocating funding to make it happen.

Since the state is envisioning high speed rail as an express service serving fewer stops, more frequent "local" Cascades service would serve a valuable purpose once the bullet train arrives, feeding the high speed hub stations and keeping the in-between cities connected. And in the interim, it would build up a base of ridership so high speed rail can hit the ground running.

State officials are aiming to complete the high speed rail service development plan by 2028. That may put the region in position to win federal funding from a new federal administration more friendly to transit than Trump has been.

Since high speed rail will likely take more than a decade to build, its success may also require a period of political stability and continued federal commitment to infrastructure investment that the United States has not seen over the last decade. But the 2026 midterm could potentially portend a larger political shift – at least if that momentum can be sustained and cultivated.
Complete WSDOT's survey by Friday, November 13.

articles.title: Community Leaders Seek Black Cultural Corridor to Sustain Yesler Way Legacy
paras: East Yesler Way, which runs through Seattle's historically Black neighborhood, is filled with numerous landmarks. Now community members want to designate the roadway as a Black cultural corridor, as a way to preserve and continue building the legacy of the Central District.

"It's not that we're necessarily creating all of these things; many of them are already here," said K. Wyking Garrett, president of the Africatown Community Land Trust (ACLT). "It's really about unboxing it, reframing it, and seeing what can be added to it to enhance it again."
The City of Seattle currently has no formal process to designate a street a cultural corridor. A cultural corridor on Yesler could likely be the first in the city.

Along with a cultural corridor on Yesler, community members want to add a festival street , which would be a space that community organizations, businesses, and residents can close for gatherings and events. A festival street must receive approval from the Seattle Department of Transportation.

The corridor on Yesler would span the entire length and would start near the waterfront, close to the new Seattle Black Panther Party Interpretive Center at 423 2nd Ave. Ext. S., and would end by Leschi Elementary School at 135 32nd Ave. So far, 30 landmarks have been identified, and there are plans to incorporate both short-term and long-term projects.

The ACLT is planning to renovate the Benu Community Home at 16th Avenue South and East Yesler Way, which is currently a shelter for adult men, into affordable housing . The Yesler Black cultural corridor is a way to bring together the existing elements and enhance the neighborhood.
"It gives us a map," said Ebony Arunga, executive director of LANGSTON , who is leading the effort to create a festival street in the Central District.

"We have big streets in the Central District: Union is a big one; Jackson is a big one; Yesler deserves its time to shine," Arunga added. "It's time for us to look at the Black history of Yesler and put it at the forefront and make sure that it's not forgotten, and that it continues to be honored."

On a walk through the neighborhood, Garrett pointed out several landmarks on 14th Avenue South and East Yesler Way, beginning with the red, green, and black stripes that adorn the crosswalk and welcome people into the Central District.

The Urban League of Metropolitan Seattle, which is the longest-standing Black-led nonprofit organization in Seattle, also sits at the intersection. Nearby, there's Washington Hall, where Black political leaders like Marcus Garvey and W.E.B. Du Bois have spoken and artists like Duke Ellington, Jimi Hendrix, and Billie Holiday have performed.

On 15th Avenue South sits Goodwill Baptist Church, a historic Black church. In the past decade, many Black-owned churches have been sold, moved, or closed entirely. Farther up on 17th Avenue South is the Langston Hughes Performing Arts Institute, originally a Jewish synagogue, which later became a hub for Black arts and culture.

Between 18th and 20th avenues sit Bryant Manor Apartments and Ashe Preparatory Early Learning, an affordable housing complex and preschool. ​​Not far away used to be R&L Home of Good Bar-B-Que, a famous Black-owned restaurant that hosted people like Martin Luther King Jr. The restaurant closed in 2018 after 66 years of business.

A couple of blocks away on East Spruce Street is the original Odessa Brown building, which still has the letters of her name engraved on it; it is now First Place Preschool. The People's Wall , a mural and the only visible reminder of the Black Panther Party's headquarters from the 1960s, is across the street. The mural was approved as an official Seattle city landmark this year.

On 20th Avenue South, both Pratt Park and Pratt Fine Arts Center are named after Edwin Pratt, a Seattle civil rights leader. At the park, some of the city's first Juneteenth celebrations were held and led by DeCharlene Williams, who also founded the Central Area Chamber of Commerce and owned a beauty salon.

The Carolyn Downs Family Medical Center and former Odessa Brown Children's Clinic are tucked in between 21st and 22nd avenues. Carolyn Downs was founded by the Seattle Black Panther Party Chapter. These clinics have provided free and affordable healthcare for low-income Black and brown residents.

One of the largest collections of African American literature and history on the West Coast is held at the Douglass-Truth library branch at 23rd Avenue and East Yesler Way. The library was originally named after Henry Yesler, one of Seattle's founders, but was later renamed in 1975 to better reflect the community.

Efforts like creating a festival street are short-term activities that can be achieved within a year to add to the corridor. Other ideas include adding artwork and murals in the community. Then, there are more ambitious projects like building affordable housing, preserving small businesses, and having more childcare centers.

Currently, plans for a festival street are centered on 17th Avenue South between East Yesler Way and South Main Street, right next to the Langston Hughes Performing Arts Institute, and would allow community members to easily close down the street for frequent public events or block parties. Other festival streets in Seattle include Canton Alley in the Chinatown-International District and South Roberto Maestas Festival Street on Beacon Hill.

"​​Whenever anyone wants to close down a street, they have to go through a lot of processes with the city and permits," Arunga said. "But when a festival street is created, that process becomes a lot easier. It's not just for LANGSTON to be able to host festivals; it's for anybody to be able to host festivals on that street."

The proposal would have to receive support from the community before the Seattle Department of Transportation approves it. Residents who live nearby will be informed, since it could affect parking and noise ordinances. Arunga said the goal is to finalize the festival street by the end of next year.

She also hopes the Langston Hughes Performing Arts Institute and the festival street can become the center of the corridor and have community members see these landmarks as places to find community events and shows.

More than 150 years ago when Seattle was founded, Henry Yesler was known as one of the early founders of the city. William Grose is said to be the city's second Black resident and was one of its wealthiest. In 1882, Grose also helped establish the Central District when he bought 12 acres from Henry Yesler for $1,000 in gold.
"Ever since Seattle was a city, there's been a Black presence in this neighborhood," Garrett said.

Since then, the Central District has become a focal point for the Black community, because, at times, there was no other place for Black people to live due to policies such as segregation and redlining. Yet in the past several decades, there has been significant change. Census data showed that some Central District census tracts were 90% Black in 1970 , but their Black population shares have dropped below 20% in more recent data.
"It's been devastating," Garrett said about the declining population of Black people in the Central District.

To counteract displacement and gentrification, Garrett said the city should invest in building affordable housing and providing pathways for home ownership for people to stay or to come back. He pointed to the Africatown Plaza at 23rd Avenue South and East Spring Street, an affordable housing building where he said 90% of the people living there have ties to the community.

The Yesler Black cultural corridor is ultimately a way to continue investing in the Central District and acknowledge the deep history of the community while still envisioning the future for the neighborhood.

"To see it and to continue to call it out — it builds an ecosystem for us to be able to utilize," Arunga said. "Yesler is the turning point of how the Central District even came to be a Black epicenter."

articles.title: Ballard Starter Line
articles.author: Martin Pagel
paras: At the Ballard Town Hall meeting Sound Transit made it clear that they do not want to make any major changes to the BLE plans to avoid starting all over with the EIS process. They did consider at some point starting with a connection between Ballard and Westlake and delay or even skip the second downtown tunnel (DSTT2). But that would require a separate operations and maintenance facility (OMF) at Interbay or connecting to the existing downtown tunnel (DSTT1). The tunnel is old and surrounding soil is unstable and therefore they concluded this would be very risky and costly. Tom Terrific however suggested a single-track maintenance tunnel connection which would connect at the end of the current tunnel by the Convention Center.

While any major design change (such as an elevated line) may jeopardize the current EIS process, implementing a project in phases is common and accepted. Not spending $8b on a second downtown tunnel at this point would allow Sound Transit to connect Ballard much earlier (in particular if paired with other measures such as automating the line or a ship canal gondola ). With all the downtown complexities it would also reduce a lot of risks. And as almost half of the tunnel is covered by funds collected in Pierce and Snohomish County and the Eastside, it may even allow Sound Transit to finish the spine earlier, a goal the Board keeps reiterating.

Sound Transit has also stated that the Ballard line is necessary to connect to the Tacoma line as an Everett to Tacoma line would get too long for operators, but they could turn Tacoma trains around at Northgate or just change operators halfway.

Sound Transit studied alternatives for a second tunnel. Either the line could connect to the existing tunnel (interlining) by tapping into the existing tunnel at Pine St and 3rd or operate as a separate line with a separate OMF at Interbay. They determined that both options would not be any cheaper than proceeding with a second tunnel. I tend to agree with the risks involved with tapping the existing tunnel for interlining. However, Tom’s suggestion for a single track to connect a Ballard line with the existing tunnel should warrant further research. To reduce operational impact, such track could be used during off-hours. It would allow maintaining trains at the SODO OMF instead of having to build a separate OMF.

Before the original tunnel was extended to Capitol Hill with a slight curve to the south, it used to have a track extending straight east of the Westlake station for trains to turn around. It might be possible to extend that tunnel portion and add a north turn. You may need to use the I-5 Express Lane exit to build such track. That track could then connect with the Ballard line roughly at the Denny station. It would be fairly long but for a maintenance track that should not matter as much.

Adding such a maintenance tunnel would be expensive, but not nearly as much as building a second tunnel or a separate Interbay OMF. I hope it would allow Sound Transit to serve Ballard well before 2042.

articles.title: Friday Roundtable: Historic Transit Investments in Puget Sound
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: The past 5 days may have been the most consequential week for transit in Puget Sound this year. Across the region, voters and elected officials decided to invest in transit for years and decades to come.

On Tuesday, voters in Seattle approved the Seattle Transit Measure (STM) with an overwhelming 72% supporting the measure. The 0.3% sales tax increase will take effect on April 1, 2027 and fund 280,000 bus trips in Seattle each year for 10 years. The measure also funds 22,000 free ORCA cards for low-income, elderly, and families with young children, maintain support for Seattle’s streetcar lines, fund spot improvements to keep buses moving, and help expedite permits and inspections for Link expansion projects in Seattle. The additional bus trips will help grow Seattle’s Very Frequent Transit Network .

In Pierce County, 58% of voters approved a significant expansion to Pierce Transit on Tuesday. The approved proposition increases the sales and use tax within the Pierce County Public Transportation Benefit Area by 0.3%. With this additional funding, Piece Transit will add four new routes, upgrade existing routes 1, 2, and 3 to Stream lines, run most routes until 10pm (8pm on Sunday), and double weekend frequencies from 1hr to 30min on 15 routes. Pierce Transit will also add seasonal and special event service when needed and expand paratransit services. The additional funding will support free fares for seniors aged 65+. Free fares for seniors will start on April 1, 2027. The new routes and other changes will be rolled out in phases to allow time for planning, hiring additional staff, and buying new buses.

On Wednesday, the Everett City Council voted unanimously voted to approve the merger of Everett Transit and Community Transit. The Community Transit Board voted to approve the merger the following day. With these votes, Everett Transit end operations on March 31, 2027. Beginning April 1, Community Transit will operate all current Everett Transit routes and CT is required to maintain or exceed the existing level of service during the transition. Over the four years following the merger, Community Transit will increase service hours in Everett by 50%. In addition, CT will add a new Zip microtransit zone in Everett by March 2028.

To fund the additional service, Community Transit’s 1.2% sales tax will replace Everett’s existing 0.6% sales tax on April 1, 2027. Fares on existing Everett Transit routes will remain at $2 until at least April 2028. Any changes to the fares will require approval from the Community Transit Board.

Community Transit will pay Everett $54.5 million for the existing transit infrastructure and to mitigate any transition costs to the City. Separately, Everett will transfer $16 million in existing transit capital reserves to support replacing buses and other equipment.

Within the past week, voters in Seattle and Pierce County and elected officials in Snohomish County decided to invest in transit. The service improvements across the region will make traveling easier and more convenient for hundreds of thousands of people everyday. As Everett and Tacoma prepare for their respective Link extensions, the decisions made this week will ensure each Link extension connects with a robust bus network.

articles.title: The 38 Best Restaurants in Seattle
articles.author: <name>Sophie Grossman</name>
paras: “Where should I eat in Seattle?” Whether you’re a first-time visitor or a lifer, that question is seemingly simple but the answers are infinitely complex. Some of the main factors to consider are the type of food, price point, neighborhood, and occasion. That’s why Eater’s map of the 38 best restaurants in Seattle exists. This curated list of suggestions attempts to capture the diversity of the food scene in the Seattle metro area, from English pubs serving cumin-y lamb neck meat pies to Indian street food takeout spots, from classic French bistros to modern sushi bars, and so much more. Every place on the list has been open for at least six months, proving its merit.

Like many menus, this map updates every quarter — removal from the Eater 38 doesn’t mean a restaurant isn’t still awesome and won’t return in the future. New to the map as of October 2026: tamale and specialty coffee haven Cafetal Quilombo Cafe, Thai dumpling hotspot E-Jae Pak Mor, and Dim Sum King, which reigns supreme in counter-service dim sum.

A note on pricing: $ means entrees are mostly under $15; $$ means entrees are mostly under $25; $$$ means entrees are priced under $35; and $$$$ means entrees are more expensive than that, or it is primarily a tasting menu restaurant. (Prices are always subject to change.)

articles.title: The Best Restaurants in Seattle’s University District
articles.author: <name>Mark DeJoy</name>
paras: The University District is frequently (and wrongly) written off as a place only college kids would want to eat; the story usually goes that it’s rife with sketchy lunch counters, nondescript multinational fast food chains, and an overabundance of boba tea joints. But the truth is that the U District is one of the city’s essential dining destinations, with a dizzying array of global cuisines concentrated on its main street, University Way (confusingly known as the Ave).

There’s Korean food, regional Chinese specialties, Indian groceries, Vietnamese kitchens, falafel windows, and more on nearly every block. And practically everything is both affordable and genuinely good, so figuring out where to eat in this neighborhood is more a matter of grappling with the paradox of choice than anything else. articles.title: Cafe Lolo Is the Neighborhood Restaurant Every Neighborhood Deserves
articles.author: <name>Kat Thompson</name>
paras: If I were to describe the perfect neighborhood restaurant, Cafe Lolo would completely fit my definition. The food is comforting and nourishing, emphasizing local ingredients, which playfully come together in a way that feels both fresh and familiar. The space is draped in natural light that’s assisted by over a dozen lamps. The inviting dining room is covered in quirky Renaissance-inspired murals that don’t feel disruptive. There are to-go meal kits available for purchase, as well as local beers. It’s an atmosphere that invites you to unwind with a bottle of wine. Owners Leah Engel, Alex Halmi, and Brett Bankson are present, not only flitting about the room, but also cooking the dishes in the kitchen and laughing with customers. If I lived in the neighborhood, just off the main drag of Capitol Hill, it’s somewhere I’d want to return to over and over again.

Cafe Lolo has an extensive wine menu and many local beers, as well as bottles in the fridge you can pick up to-go. Although yes, the wine list — which includes just one glass from Washington, and more options from Oregon and Europe) — is worth perusing, the nonalcoholic tisanes are also made from seasonal ingredients. The strawberry rhubarb soda I had on my visit was effervescent and floral without an overpowering sweetness.

Like the rest of the menu, dessert will change pending seasons — but don’t skip it. My visit included a celebration of ripe, macerated strawberries over a semolina olive oil cake, which had a buttery crust and a tender interior crumb. There was also a scoop of rhubarb sorbet; light, sweet, and sharp.

articles.title: The Best Restaurants in Ballard
articles.author: <name>Mark DeJoy</name>
paras: Once a quiet working-class Nordic-American neighborhood, Ballard is now a nightlife, shopping, and restaurant destination. Boutiques and cocktail bars line Ballard Avenue (home to one of Seattle’s few year-round farmers markets ), and townhomes and high-rises have taken the place of single-family homes. Some of the best restaurants and bars in the city can be found here, along with almost (almost!) too many breweries , which is why if you walk far enough inland you can literally smell the hops. Where else in Seattle can you find Detroit-style pizza, Sri Lankan cocktails, and a congee specialist?
